This paper introduces a new notion of consistency for random dynamic systems, which we call $\mathcal{A}$-consistency. We demonstrate that $\mathcal{A}$-consistency is a more versatile concept than asymptotic uniqueness. Furthermore, we develop a method to check for $\mathcal{A}$-consistency by examining unique solutions under slightly larger conditions, thus providing a practical approach for verification. We apply this method to two specific examples, one of which involves a mean-field model with interactions, and the other a queueing process, thereby establishing asymptotic behavior for these scenarios. We also propose a process, which we call the Q-process, and prove that it achieves $\mathcal{A}$-consistency. We further show that the Q-process can be used as a convergence rate tool, allowing for the derivation of convergence rates for systems with symmetric right-hand side functions. We illustrate the efficiency of this method by calculating precise convergence rates for systems with jump Markov processes and multiplicative noise. Additionally, we apply the methods developed in this paper to various benchmark examples, thereby providing a unified framework for analyzing these scenarios, and we calculate precise convergence rates for systems with jump dynamics, confirming known results, and deriving new findings. Furthermore, we propose a method to obtain sharp convergence rates for systems with additive noise. We collect and summarize our key findings in a concise table. We introduce a novel technique for obtaining precise asymptotic estimates by integrating the measure of a flow. We apply this integration method to a counterexample that challenges the existing notion that unique solutions lead to asymptotic stability. We use the Q-process to analyze this counterexample and demonstrate that it yields precise asymptotic estimates, thereby providing a more versatile approach than currently available methods. We collect and summarize our key findings in a concise table. We further show that the Q-process can be used to derive mean-convergence for systems with common arrival and departure processes, and we apply this result to a counterexample that challenges the existing notion of asymptotic uniqueness. The effect of particle adhesion on the surface tissues of living organisms at body temperature has garnered considerable interest in recent years. In this context, we investigate the thermal acceleration of nanoparticle attachment to a graphene surface driven by electrical impulses. By leveraging surface plasmon resonance, we manage to boost the attachment rate by several orders of magnitude. Additionally, we find that the size and shape of the nanoparticles significantly impact the thermal energy generated and affect the attachment mechanism. Our research employs atomic force microscopy to observe the real-time adhesion process, providing valuable insights into the behavior of nanoparticles in this context. This study lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of nanoparticle interaction with biological cells at room temperature. Furthermore, the techniques and strategies outlined herein may facilitate the development of novel, graphene-based tools for biomedical applications. Since room-temperature surface adhesion is often weak and insufficient for many applications, we explore the possibility of using electrical pulses to boost nanoparticle attachment. By combining this approach with surface plasmon resonance, we achieve a 10 orders-of-magnitude increase in attachment rate and demonstrate real-time, atomic-force-microscopy observations of the process. This facilitated study of nanoparticle shape and size effects could lead to the development of surface-plasmon-assisted tools for biomedical applications. Ultimately, we show that a controlled, electrical pulse is all that is needed to activate nanoparticle adhesion. This simple, yet effective, mechanism could enable the development of novel, graphene-based tools for manipulating nanoparticle interaction with biological cells. By leveraging electrical pulses and surface plasmon resonance, we achieve a 10 orders-of-magnitude increase in nanoparticle adhesion, setting the stage for novel applications in biomedicine and nanotechnology. In a test of conformal symmetry, we employ the conformal bootstrap technique to analyze one-dimensional supersymmetric systems, specifically the Wess-Zumino model, which is known to be consistently non-supersymmetric due to monodromy inconsistencies. By bootstrapping these systems, we find that they are invariant under global $R$-symmetry, and we derive new constraints on their four-point correlation functions, incorporating higher-spin operators with two and four supersymmetry indices. Furthermore, we verify that these operators' mixing is zero, and we discuss how our findings relate to the monodromy property, ultimately amplifying previous theoretical considerations with rigorous bootstrapping outcomes. Additionally, we provide a monodromy-imperfection-free four-point function example, and we anticipate that our results will yield valuable insights for other one-dimensional supersymmetric systems. Critical examination of our analysis also reveals potential issues arising from the truncation of operator spaces, suggesting that monodromy imperfections might actually be constrained within a narrow range, and we leave the resolution of these concerns for future research. Lastly, in a related development, we extend our knowledge on the Wess-Zumino model by applying the conformal bootstrap technique to its related system, specifically the free fermion, which is known to be monodromy-invariant due to its fermionic nature. By testing global $R$-symmetry in this system, we derive new constraints on its correlation functions, verify the nonmixing of specific operators, and provide a monodromy-perfection-free four-point function example, thereby expanding our understanding of one-dimensional supersymmetric systems via the conformal bootstrap technique. Overall, this study offers a fresh perspective on the monodromy property through the conformal bootstrap technique, and we expect future research to build upon these theoretical considerations and outcomes. We investigate the multiple time, discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process with periodic boundaries, focusing on systems with a specific detailed balance condition. For systems having an integer number of sites and a non-divisible bias, we develop a formula for the probability distribution of a system with multiple sites, demonstrating that it follows a product of independent Gaussian distributions. This result is validated through comparison with the outcomes of exact analytic methods proven for specific cases and by matching moments derived from the generated distributions with those obtained from alternative methods. Additionally, we propose a scheme for obtaining distribution functions in systems with irregular time steps. We further examine the behavior of multiple exclusion processes, investigating how certain mean response properties change in response to periodic driving forces. For systems in a detailed balance condition, we demonstrate that the mean current can be expressed as the product of two one-dimensional marginals, while for non-equilibrium systems, we obtain a closed-form expression for the mean response and verify it against results obtained from exact analytic methods, as well as by calculating it directly from the generated probability distributions. These findings are confirmed to be universal, applicable to different representations of the exclusion process. Laparoscopic surgery has become a common practice, allowing for minimal invasion while providing surgeons with clear visual guidance.  The development of advanced technologies has enhanced this method, enabling more sophisticated surgical procedures.  Despite its effectiveness, a potential risk of smoke interference to laparoscopic vision during these procedures needs to be addressed.  To mitigate this, a pre-surgical test can identify if a patient's smoke production could compromise vision during surgery.  The purpose of this study is to explore whether image processing techniques can utilize existing surgical images to identify potential smoke hazards.  The research presents a novel approach, focusing on the role of image processing in predicting smoke images.  The results demonstrate that, although the existing surgical database includes smoke images, they are infrequently encountered.  To improve the model's performance, the researchers applied image filtering, revealing that bias in the original data set actually becomes an advantage when cleaned.  The outcomes indicate that a cleaner approach can lead to better outcomes in identifying smoke images.  The researchers conclude that image processing may be beneficial in predicting smoke images, allowing for more accurate detection through enhanced visibility.  The study is published in the journal of Surgical Endoscopy.  The developed code is available on GitHub, while the data used is obtainable from the Dutch Uro Radiology database.  The researchers responsible for the data can be contacted via mail at urorad@radb.nl to obtain the data.  The relevant surgical information is described in the supplied file. The researchers conducted 15 tests to assess the image processing model, using random masks and filters to simulate smoke images.  The outcome is presented in a bar chart showing the frequency of predicted smoke images.  The researchers evaluated the image processing model using frequency and probability maps, demonstrating a noticeable improvement with image processing.  The outcome is presented in a graph showing the before and after effect of image processing on the surgical database.  The researchers applied a binary classification system, training the model to distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images.  The outcome is presented in two graphs showing the accuracy and confusion matrices.  The researchers used the Dutch Uro Radiology database, comprising laparoscopic surgical images, along with corresponding patient metadata.  The outcome is presented in a graph showing the distribution of the Dutch Uro Radiology database.  The researchers utilized image processing techniques, specifically filtering, to examine its effect on predicting smoke images.

A vital application of autonomous vehicles is going to be resilient positioning and tracking, which has seen significant advancement through various sensors including deep neural networks and adaptive algorithms. Although numerous localization and tracking algorithms have been developed, they have not been able to cope with the level of reliability required for autonomous operations. In this paper, a unique technique combining an adaptive algorithm with a predictive damped method is introduced to provide resilient state estimation for autonomous vehicles using radio-based sensing data. By modeling dependence among sensors, the technique is able to provide a unified framework for calculating the confidence level of individual sensors as well as their combined confidence level. A virtual communication channel is used to represent sensor confidence, with a weighted average formula determining the combined confidence level. This technique is applied to a radio-based localization and tracking system and tested with data containing both intentional and unintentional interference. Results show that the technique is able to provide robust state estimation even in the presence of compromised sensors with noticeable accuracy and very low error rates compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the technique is capable of detecting and mitigating the impact of malicious sensors with an error rate of 99.9%, making it an extremely effective tool for resilient sensing and control applications. The $W^{\pm}Z$ particle production process has been analyzed from proton-proton collisions recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider between 2015 and 2018 at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy.  Within the framework of the Standard Model, the $W^{\pm}Z$ production properties are well understood and account for a substantial portion of the visible two gauge boson channel.  Through data analysis of 139/fb of recorded events, deviations from the Standard Model are found in the joint polarization states of the $W^{\pm}Z$ system, particularly in $Z$ particle polarization, with an observed excess of 0.7(0.6) standard deviations for right-handedly polarized $W^+$ ($Z$) particles.  Meanwhile, no notable deviations are detected in $W$ particle polarization.  Additionally, standardized limits are placed on Beyond-Standard-Model models proposing gauge boson anomalous parity constraints, with some models' parameters modulated by a factor of 10^(-15) or more considering the measured field interactions.  These findings mark significant advancements in the detection of joint gauge boson polarization states and anomalous parity models within the $W^{\pm}Z$ particle production process. Research on the Cotton tensor has resumed with renewed interest in this object, which was initially proposed over 80 years ago as a potential alternative to the Weyl tensor for describing curvature. This object remains poorly understood despite being linked to conformal gravity. In this article, we aim to enhance knowledge of the Cotton tensor by examining its properties and how it relates to standard gravity descriptors, with a focus on its connection to the Weyl tensor and conformal metrics. Additionally, we investigate its significance in conformal gravity, highlighting its significance in this theory and discussing its implications in this context. Furthermore, we explore solutions to four-dimensional conformal gravity that feature either a vanishing or constant Cotton tensor, and discuss these solutions as examples of conformally riemannian metrics. These solutions indicate that the Cotton tensor can serve as a useful tool for identifying these special metrics. Lastly, we investigate three-dimensional conformal gravity, and reveal that this theory admits a variant that resembles teleparallel gravity, with the Cotton tensor acting as an equivalent descriptor of curvature in this variant. Our research thus demonstrates that the Cotton tensor can act as a unified descriptor of curvature that is capable of portraying both standard and conformally extended gravity, as well as a potential alternative to the Weyl tensor in this realm. In particular, we show that the Cotton tensor can be used to express the Einstein action in four and three dimensions, indicating that it can act as a potential source for these fields in these contexts. Our results provide a foundation for further research into the Cotton tensor and its potential applications in teleparallel gravity, which may offer insights into the formulation of this theory. With these advances, we hope to stimulate renewed interest in the Cotton tensor as a versatile tool for studying gravity. Our research may also contribute to the development of connections between standard and conformally extended gravity, which may hold important implications for understanding these theories. Finally, we hope that our findings will prove useful in future research into the Cotton tensor and its potential applications in conformal gravity. Our central conclusion is that the Cotton tensor can be used to describe the curvature of various manifolds, which may be of use in studying these theories. Our results may also indicate that the Cotton tensor can be used to study gravity in four and three dimensions, which may prove to be a valuable area of research in these contexts. We introduce a visual representation of proof trees for Coq proofs, which can be exported in various formats including PDF, HTML, and SVG. Our tool also allows for interacting with the proofs through hyperlinks. Furthermore, the source code is publicly accessible on GitHub. This visualisation method employs a novel technique for translating Coq proofs into proof nets, combining elements of proof normalisation and proof translation. To achieve this, we adopt a proof net structure analogous to that used in Girard's unit-free proof nets and incorporate a method for generating visual representations of these nets. Our tool includes features for visualising and navigating the diagrams, as well as a reviewer mode that redacts unnecessary details in the proof. The convergence of GMRES can be unpredictable outside of the cone $x\perp_{\mathcal{N}(M^T)) x$ and is sensitive to initial guesses and the conditioning of $M$. The strict obliquity condition $x\perp_{N(M^T)}x$ is challenging to fulfill at each iteration, prompting the search for alternative criteria to terminate GMRES early and avoid unnecessary computations. This paper presents a novel criterion based on the edge length of the polyhedral cone $C$, which is a key component in IPMs, and shows that its implementation is feasible within the context of IPMs. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective in interior point methods for both linear and nonlinear optimization problems. Additionally, the research highlights the underappreciated role of the Firouzi-Razavi inner product in optimizing algorithms. The author also suggests modifying the inner product to enhance the performance of optimization software. The research further investigates an alternative termination condition for GMRES based on the residual norm in relation to the polyhedral cone's edge length. The study offers a thorough analysis of the dynamics between the residual norm and the edge length as an affordable substitute for monitoring the distance to the center of the polyhedral cone. The results demonstrate that this approximation is informative and allows for early termination of GMRES, thereby significantly reducing the number of iterations. The research also verifies that the proposed method maintains equivalence to the standard interior point method in terms of both primal and dual optimality. The algorithm has been independently tested in MATLAB to confirm that it outperforms standard methods, with a particular advantage observed when dealing with sparse and well-conditioned systems. The research further extends its findings to the more complex and widely used Primal Dual Interior Point Method (PDIPM) to compare its performance with a modified version that utilizes the proposed termination criterion. The results show that using the proposed criterion with PDIPM yields comparable outcomes in terms of both efficiency and complexity, offering a promising future direction for further research and development. investigates the behavior of the $t+\bar{b}+j+\mbox{X}$ and $t\bar{t}+j+\mbox{X}$

evaluates the forward and backward $b$-jet pull. This research also examines 
$J_z$ conservation in top quark events and finds that nuclear effects do not

Research has developed sophisticated conceptually grounded methods for detecting potential issues within business processes by analyzing events that occur during their execution. These methods provide descriptive process mining, highlighting patterns and trends, and predictive process mining, forecasting future events. In contrast, few methods effectively guide process correction by identifying issues and suggesting modifications. This discrepancy motivates our work, which aims to advance procedure monitoring by incorporating prescriptive capabilities. By leveraging organizational standards and constraints, we introduce an approach called Prescriptive Procedure Monitoring (PPM) that employs procedures modelled with constraints and optimizes event processing to identify issues and suggest corrections. Our approach is generalized into three distinct instances, each incorporating a specific type of procedure model. Empirical validation through case studies demonstrates PPM's effectiveness in detecting problems and proposing fixes, underscoring its potential to enhance procedure monitoring with prescriptive capabilities. The source code for our approach has been made available on GitHub at the specified URL. Future research directions are also outlined, focusing on further developing procedure monitoring with prescriptive capabilities. Keywords: Procedure Monitoring, Business Processes, Constraints, Optimization, Machine Learning, (Con)Constraints, Business Process Mining.

In the realm of opinion dynamics, individuals form opinions based on their own beliefs, as well as external influences like social networks and exposure to varying information sources. Traditional models assume a fixed framework and universal access to opinion sources. Conversely, a recent theory explores the consequences of a shifting social structure in response to opinion changes. This research builds upon that framework by incorporating a more realistic approach, one where the structure adapts to opinion distributions, while also imposing constraints on opinion source accessibility. To achieve this, we incorporate confidence intervals into opinion dynamics models, enabling a more nuanced examination of uncertainty in opinion measurement. Furthermore, our opinion distribution expressions exhibit asymptotic stability, where opinions converge uniformly as time progresses. Lastly, numerical simulations are employed to investigate how opinion distributions respond to varying numbers of observable opinions over time. Notably, results indicate that opinions become more concentrated as the number of observable opinions increases. In contrast, a greater number of uncertain opinions leads to more dispersed opinions. This fundamental finding applies across different models, demonstrating that a more comprehensive understanding of opinion dynamics is attainable when distribution variability is considered. To achieve this understanding, we incorporate a step-by-step modeling approach, one where structural changes are paired with dynamic opinions, each governed by formal equations. By acknowledging and accommodating uncertainty, our research presents a more inclusive outlook on dynamic public opinion. In doing so, we establish a groundwork for studying opinion dynamics that could be applied in real-world settings, expanding beyond the scope of this research. Additionally, our model provides a potential framework for tackling more intricate problems, such as modeling competition between different opinion groups, as well as exploring potential applications of our coupled opinion and structural models in fields like sociology and economics. Ultimately, this work presents a unified theoretical framework for examining shifting social structures and their impact on public opinion, one that could be utilized for creating predictive models and informing policy decisions in the realm of public opinion dynamics. A study discovered that deep learning can create accurate representations of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract for virtual navigation systems, enabling real-time guidance within the surgical field. This is achieved through a novel, automated segmentation of the upper GI canal on 2D endoscopic videos. The researchers employed a fully convolutional neural network, training it with a large video dataset, resulting in rapid, in-field calculations even with limited resources. Notably, the accuracy of the segmentation was increased by incorporating spatial constraints, ensuring the model's reliability across various anatomical variations. The outcome allowed for development of a simple, real-time navigation system guiding the endoscope through the upper GI canal. The results indicate potential for the model to accurately map the lower GI canal as well, enabling a broad range of clinical applications. The work is presently being translated into a commercial product for clinical use. The source code used in the study has been publicly released on GitHub, allowing other researchers to replicate the results. The dataset utilized for training the model can be accessed through the USC-SIPI repository after registering. The model can be applied on Windows, macOS, and Linux systems using a USB stick, with instructions available on GitHub. The researchers are now working on expanding the model to segment the lower GI canal and abdominal organs, aiming to introduce a system that assists in monitoring the progression of digestive diseases. The model may also enable virtual navigation for surgical procedures and therapeutic agents targeting specific canals within the GI tract. The accuracy of the model in mapping the upper GI canal was evaluated using the Dice score, a metric showing high coefficients (mean: 0.925, range: 0.861 to 0.985) for the cohort study. The segmentation results were then normalized to account for the varied sizes of the canals, revealing strong correlations with the ground truth values (mean: 0.953, range: 0.891 to 0.976). The researchers further analyzed the model's performance, assessing its reliability across different regions of the GI canal and its ability to detect canals within the videos. The accuracy of the model was found to decrease slightly when testing was conducted on videos shot by cameras with different fields of view, but this effect was minimized through the use of spatial constraints. The model enabled real-time calculations, allowing it to process one frame per millisecond, and its parameters were found to be optimal for the upper GI canal, with further training yielding poorer results. The idea that massive exoplanets might be rare due to migration from the outer planet regime has been supported by several studies. This hypothesis is tested using a comprehensive dataset of exoplanets discovered through the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity program. By examining correlations between inner and outer planet masses, we investigate the validity of this concept. Our analysis reveals no substantial evidence to support this theory, as it applies to the CORALIE/HARPS sample. Furthermore, we observe that planets in the mass range of 0.3 to 10 solar masses are discovered at a steady rate, suggesting a lack of a desert region. In line with previous findings, we also demonstrate that inner and outer planets often coexist and share similar mass characteristics. The discovery of this correlation challenges the notion of planetary escapism and highlights the importance of future discoveries to clarify the formation and loss mechanisms of exoplanets. To address the problem of attention distribution imbalance in vision-language understanding, we introduce a novel approach based on the principle of information theory. We propose a dual-head architecture where two separate attention mechanisms are trained simultaneously to optimize their collective entropy, thereby constraining their behavior and preventing over-specialization. This technique allows us to regulate the behavior of individual attention heads and improve overall performance. We tested our approach on multiple benchmark datasets and achieved impressive results, setting new standards for accuracy and providing a valuable framework for understanding attention mechanisms. Specifically, we demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on the VQLP and VQLP+ datasets, surpassing previous benchmarks by significant margins. Moreover, we validated the effectiveness of our method through rigorous ablation studies and provided insightful analysis of its contributions. The code for our approach is openly available on the GITHub repository for easy reproduction of results. Additionally, we conducted thorough evaluations of computational complexity and memory requirements, ensuring the scalability of our method for real-world applications. Considering the popularity of attention mechanisms among deep learning practitioners, we believe our technique offers highly accessible and adaptable solution to the problem of attention specialization. Moreover, as attention models continue to evolve for various task, our method may be generalized to address similar challenges and provide a unified framework for regulating the behavior of multiple attention heads. The proposed technique can be potentially applied to other challenging tasks, such as image and text manipulation, language modeling, and generation of coherent images, among others. Moreover, as vision-language models are increasingly employed in real-time video processing and multimedia content analysis, our method may be applied to address the problem of attention specialization in these domains, thereby enabling more robust and coherent video understanding. Furthermore, as deep learning models continue to evolve rapidly, our approach can be potentially generalized to address the problem of attention specialization in more advanced architectures and task settings, thereby enhancing their performance and providing a deeper understanding of their behavior. The proposed technique offers a novel approach to regulating the behavior of attention mechanisms, providing insights into the role of individual heads and the collective contributions of shared information, thereby enabling more effective vision-language understanding models. The presented results validate the importance of regulating the behavior of attention mechanisms to achieve state-of-the-art performance, providing valuable insights for the deep learning community and paving the way for further research and development. The stability of dark matter (DM) at the weak scale can be achieved through the suppression of the Yukawa coupling that controls the DM particle's interaction with normal matter. In most models, this suppression is model-dependent, but a new class of models offers a hope for a more universal solution. Compressed DM models, characterized by an approximate $Z_2$ symmetry, provide a framework for the weak-sector Dark Matter to interact with the hidden sector via a Yukawa coupling. For a range of model parameters, this interaction can result in the formation of bound states within the hidden sector, leading to the creation of a lightweight pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson. Depending on the value of the Yukawa coupling, this boson may either dominate DM composition or significantly influence the dark matter direct detection experiments' results. The models in this class can be tested through various phenomena, such as production rates in future collider experiments, constraints on the decay of DM particles, and the influence of DM interactions on the sun's long-term energy output. The potential for discovery is substantial, offering a chance to explain not only dark matter's presence but also the solar neutrino problem through the model's ability to set a limit on the value of the angle theta_13 in electroweak interactions. The proposed model also offers an explanation for the observed difference between the dark matter and baryon number densities. The models in this class can be further categorized based on the value of the compressed DM mass, which determines the behavior of the model's parameters in the (m_{Z2}, k_{Y}) plane. For example, a model with an undercompressed DM results in a model where the model's parameters converge to a specific point, while a model with a supercompressed DM leads to a relationship between the model parameters that forms a curve in this parameter space. The models with a value of the compressed DM mass roughly equal to the top quark mass result in a pattern of lines and critical points in this parameter space. Deep recurrent neural networks (RNNs) serve as learning machines in various cognitive tasks and can mimic specific neurological disorders, making them an attractive model for research. However, their applicability is limited by their tendency to fall into local minima during training, which slows learning. Unlike traditional fully-connected networks, RNNs can't leverage the benefits of sparsity, which can improve model efficiency and learning performance. This study introduces a fixed-sparse structure in RNNs, allowing the creation of large models with variable parameters, while exploiting sparsity for improved training efficiency. The results show that our method surpasses current benchmarks in several benchmark tasks, while also producing models that mimic real brain mechanisms. Furthermore, our method exhibits superior performance to previous approaches in learning rules in synthetic and natural tasks, which are crucial for understanding brain plasticity. The developed models show potential in bridging the gap between neural networks and neurobiology, while also yielding insights into brain learning processes. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ccorreia87/Sparse-RNNs.EFRN.

This study presents a method to enhance the performance of medical image registration, particularly by leveraging symmetry properties in feature detection for picture volumes. Building on the SP-Symmetry framework, we incorporate these properties into the 3D SIFT feature detection process. As a result, we introduce a novel and efficient feature, SP-SIFT, which exhibits invariance to spatial transformations and symmetry across dimensions. To optimize computational costs, we also offer a simplified version, spSIFT. To demonstrate the potential of this approach, we introduce a registration pipeline using sparse point correspondences derived from spSIFT, which achieves a significant performance gain on challenging, highly deformable datasets in comparative evaluations. Additionally, we present a learning-based pipeline using a Siamese network to speed up sparse correspondence creation, yielding results comparable to optimal manual sparse correspondence selection. Our proposed method, SP-SIFT, along with associated code, has been made publicly available on GitHub. Experimental data and source codes are accessible via the following links: the code: https://github.com/IMST-DAEDALUS/SP-SIFT, the dataset: https://github.com/IMST-DAEDALUS/3B-SIFT-learner, and the dataset: https://daten.unibas.ch/datasets/DAEDALUS-2022-UNIBAS-DAEDALUS/. In addition, the associated dataset of generated spSIFT correspondences can be accessed via https://daten.unibas.ch/datasets/DAEDALUS-2023-UNIBAS-DAEDALUS. Experimental results show the substantial spSIFT correspondence coverage of diverse organs across diverse patient groups due to its robust performance. However, it may fail in extremely low-contrast scenarios. Consequently, we introduce a complementary method based on an extended symmetry-aware SIFT (spSIFT) to enhance its potential in such situations. Moreover, we present a novel strategy for efficiently training binary classifiers using SP-SIFT features for distinguishing between organs and background based on a novel, simplified descriptor: spSIFT-lean. Using our method, we achieve an accuracy of 98.6% in identifying liver and spleen organs based on an evaluation of ten distinct, highly deformable liver and spleen trajectories selected from our registered patient series, demonstrating potential for improving current, error-prone manual background removal methods. Consequently, we present a new learning paradigm using a general approach to efficiently create sparse correspondences for robust image registration, which significantly outperforms current efficient sparse correspondence creation

We analyzed a unique binary system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which consists of two ancient stars that orbit every 40.5 minutes. By examining the light emitted from this binary, we identified the behaviors of its component stars. Notably, the larger star has a natural oscillation that lasts around 9-10 minutes, causing occasional and subtle changes in the system's overall brightness. This auto-periodic variation plays a crucial role in understanding the system's overall light output. After processing the data and accounting for the smaller star's effects, we found that the larger star undergoes significant changes in its physical characteristics, which are visible as changes in its light output. This phenomenon is marked by a particular type of variation known as the 'white dwarf pulsation', which is relatively rare in its class. Moreover, our research provides evidence of another type of oscillation, which may be attributed to the movement of internal fluids or other factors. This study is one of the first to document this particular oscillation in a given system. By cross-referencing our findings with various models, we were able to gain insights into the binary's physical behavior and its underlying structure. This information has further enhanced our understanding of binary systems like SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, which are expected to exhibit similar characteristics due to their ancient origins and similar compositions. This study disabled the previous findings on the system's timing behavior and instead presented new data, which is based on our analysis of the full data set provided by the ULTRACAM camera. Our research revealed systematic errors of 0.0001 minutes for the system's period timing data. This study is a comprehensive exploration of the full behavioral spectrum of a binary system that was previously investigated in research by Pons et al. (2018). By comparing our findings with their study, we were able to reveal differences and similarities between the ULTRACAM and SDSS timing data. Notably, both studies revealed identical systematic errors and similar behavioral patterns. This similarity further validates the accuracy of our period timing data, which shows that the binary's behavior remains relatively consistent over time. This study is a further validation of the wide applicability of the timing data obtained through ULTRACAM camera observations. This study re-evaluates the process of global averaging using a perspective-based approach and develops a new global averaging algorithm, OT-GA, which is grounded in optimal transport theory. OT-GA is shown to converge asymptotically to the true mean under specific conditions, and its convergence is demonstrated using a convergence rate analysis. In addition, OT-GA is rigorously proven to achieve an optimal bias in its estimates, and this bias is quantified through a mean squared error (MSE) analysis. Our empirical evaluations confirm that OT-GA surpasses the efficiency of the current state-of-the-art methods, particularly in distributed deep neural network training scenarios. OT-GA is further complemented by a variant, OT-GA-D, which enhances its performance by leveraging an accelerated optimal transport technique to dynamic average. OT-GA-D is demonstrated to yield superior performance and high acceleration rates compared to the current state-of-the-art methods in communication-efficient distributed CNN training. All of our source code is openly accessible on GitHub, specifically at the following links: OT-GA: https://github.com/jbie-ncsu/OT-GA and OT-GA-D: https://github.com/jbie-ncsu/OT-GA-D. Furthermore, our OT-GA and OT-GA-D results are also publicly available on NeurIPS 2021 Dashboard: https://neurips2021.grandom.org/OT-GA and https://neurips2021.grandom.org/OT-GA-D. Our OT-GA-D results are also available on the Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) Library: https://erm-lab.github.io/OT-GA. OT-GA can be utilized in a wide range of distributed learning applications, such as training deep neural networks, computing statistical aggregates, and performing all-reduce operations. It is compatible with various communication libraries, including AllReduce, Ring, and NCCL. OT-GA and OT-GA-D have been evaluated on different datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet. OT-GA-D has specifically demonstrated exceptional performance and high acceleration rates compared to the current state-of-the-art methods in communication-efficient distributed ResNet50 training on ImageNet. This research aims to derive flat rotational surfaces in the form of a parallel plane within a 4-dimensional Euclidean space, using a parameterization method that considers a pointwise 1-type Gauss function. To demonstrate the existence of these flat rotational surfaces, we present an example consisting of a standard parallel plane coupled with a rotational component, characterized by a constant angle $\alpha$ and a linear function $u=x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta$ in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^4$, where $\theta$ depends on $u$. The paper further illustrates that these flat rotational surfaces can be generalized using a 1-type Gauss function in $\mathbb{E}^4$, parameterized by the variables $s$ and $t$, which in turn enables the generation of these flat surfaces for any angle $\alpha$ and these surfaces are simultaneously 1-type and flat surfaces. Additionally, we demonstrate that the solutions for $\alpha$ and the parameterization functions $u=s\cos A + t\sin A$ and $u=s\sin A - t\cos A$ exist for specific values of $A$ in the range $[0,2\pi]$. Deep neural network training on vast image datasets has been facilitated by using pre-trained models, often developed on classification datasets like ImageNet. Yet, for semantic segmentation tasks, alternative approaches have emerged that leverage training on vast synthetic datasets or unsupervised depth estimation data instead. We key into this unconventional method and find through experimentation that training a model to predict depth from a single image can be beneficial for performing semantic segmentation. To achieve this, we employ unsupervised depth estimation techniques and find that models pre-trained in this way exhibit improved performance on various segmentation tasks, surpassing the conventional method of being pre-trained on ImageNet. This novel approach is found to be adaptable to various models and scenarios, and we also identify potential limitations and areas for further exploration. Additionally, we open-source our code to enable replication of this research for similar tasks and applications. From an computational efficiency standpoint, we find that training on depth estimation targets allows models to converge at a much faster rate, utilizing monitoring metrics such as pixel accuracy and mean intersection over union (mIoU). We also collect and provide supplemental analysis, including training and validation metrics, for our method and other approaches for thorough comparison. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the models pre-trained using our technique can be effectively fine-tuned using a limited number of labeled real images, resulting in substantial improvements. Specifically, by utilizing 10% of the training data, we observe an average increase of over 5% in mIoU compared to models fine-tuned using ImageNet pre-trained models. To validate the efficacy of our technique in various real-world settings, we also perform tests on datasets obtained from the COCO-Stuff challenge and the KITTI360 benchmark, and find that it yields significant improvements across multiple evaluation metrics, including mIoU, pixel accuracy, and M-1 F-measure. Moreover, we devise a novel metric for comparing the semantic coherence of depth-based and ImageNet pre-trained models, and find that the former consistently outperforms the latter. To facilitate reproducibility, we open-source our code and provide the training and validation metrics for each model setup. We also offer an model that can be downloaded for evaluation and testing, giving credit to the original authors for providing the code. We expect that our technique will be universally applicable to various deep neural network models, and based on our results so far, it appears that it will be a robust and efficient method for performing semantic segmentation. The rise of neural story generation systems poses significant challenges to their broader adoption: these models often require extensive knowledge of a specific subject area, like space exploration, to generate coherent stories. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a novel approach called TCube, a time-series storytelling framework that can create engaging narratives without needing domain-specific training. TCube employs a novel story structure that integrates three key components: (1) time-series segmentation; (2) story framing; and (3) narrative construction. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we've conducted experiments involving both human evaluations and metrics-based assessments, revealing that TCube produces better stories with higher coherence, consistency, and overall quality. Moreover, we've analyzed the results of our human evaluations to identify the strengths and weaknesses of our approach. The proposed method showcases a promising future for developing stories on various topics. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/jaychauhan87/TCube. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find new periodic measures that are mildly exotic. These measures are characterized by a unique feature: the periodicity is valid only for a specific subset of lattice points, while the system's spin values on unique paths can vary freely. The existence of these measures is proven through a straightforward argument, and we further demonstrate that they can be extended to represent a significant portion of all possible measures on the lattice. The periodic measures we've found can also be analyzed in terms of the system's thermodynamic properties. Specifically, we show that the free energy associated with these measures exhibits a singular behavior as the temperature increases. This result is consistent with findings from previous studies on measure of complexity for Ising models on Cayley trees. The thermodynamic singularities resulting from these measures can be distinguished from those caused by standard periodic Gibbs measures using numerical methods. The analysis involves a detailed evaluation of the thermodynamic properties of the system, including the specific heat and susceptibility, as a function of temperature. client software accessing a centralized database for discovering and managing
distributed computations. Despite their efforts, these projects continue to struggle
with maintaining a sufficient workforce. The main obstacle lies in the outdated client
technology, limiting its usability and making it unattractive for potential volunteers.
To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, Pando, which allows existing
clients to leverage web browser resources for computation. The main objective of Pando
is to attract fresh volunteers, while ensuring seamless integration for existing users.
The key component of our solution is a browser-based micro-service, capable of
automating deployment, configuration, and management of volunteer computing resources.
By focusing on BOINC as our primary use case, we successfully implemented a functioning
prototype, which demonstrates the feasibility of Pando for combining browser and
main system resources in volunteer computing operations. The results of our initial
testing indicate significant improvements in overall throughput, with average system
loads remaining within predetermined limits defined by the administrators. Moreover,
Pando's innovative approach allows for dynamic adjustments in the way Pando leverages
browser and system resources, thereby enabling improved flexibility in load management. 

In this research, we introduce the concepts of
  - Pando's micro-services architecture for dynamic load balancing and adaptation,
  - efficient Pando deployment through local development and staging,
  - effective bootstrapping and resolution mechanisms for handling failures and
  - Pando's optimal resource management strategy for maximum performance and
  - latent load management to prevent overload and achieve the best possible
  performance when using a large number of units. 

Through numerical analysis with BOINC as our primary platform, we examine the following
variables: the number of computations per unit of time, the overall system load,
resource utilization, and the number of active volunteers for two test scenarios: a
small-scale (local) setup and a large-scale deployment. The data from these experiments
validate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving higher computational output,
balanced system performance, and optimal volunteer utilization for both small and
large-scale applications. Moreover, our research highlights the promise of Pando in

By employing a fractal-related method, we demonstrate that the unique invariant measure for this transformation, which we'll call an intermediate beta shift, can be expressed as a measure on the Cantor set defined by a specific recursive procedure. This method enables us to count the asymptotic rate at which pairs of orbiting points converge, resulting in a consistent estimate for the entropy of the intermediate beta shift. data itself. However, potential data breaches from the training servers remain a

This research introduces a novel automated approach for evaluating embedded system operators using hardware description languages. By leveraging a domain-specific language database and hardware description language parser, our method automates the translation and synthesis of operators and inputs, enabling fast and efficient simulation-based evaluation. To accommodate hardware constraints, we implement a streamlined simulation framework and introduce a novel benchmark generator for evaluating embedded system operators. Evaluations on various benchmarks demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances evaluation speed and reduces resource usage, while approximately matching the performance of manual designs. Moreover, we introduce a first public benchmark set for evaluating embedded system operators, consisting of 107 benchmarks derived from existing literature and new proposals. This benchmark set, which can be accessed through our project website, supports evaluation of embedded system operators and facilitates replication of our research findings. Furthermore, we introduce a first benchmark set focused on evaluating folding techniques for embedded system operators. This benchmark set, which can also be accessed on our project website, supports evaluation of folding techniques and enables comparison of their performance on actual benchmarks. In addition to introducing our method and benchmark sets, we conduct a thorough analysis of the impact of hardware architectures on folding techniques and present our experimental results. To facilitate replication of our research, we make public our code, benchmark sets, and simulation framework, which can be accessed through our project website under the specified URL. This project aims to contribute to the development of automated design tools for evaluating and processing data on embedded systems, promoting research in this area and shedding light on the impact of hardware architectures on folding techniques. To demonstrate the practicality of our approach, we apply it to evaluate and synthesize a real-world JPEG decoder operator on actual hardware, achieving speeds of up to 45.8 Mbps in software-based implementations and pinpointing the performance bottlenecks on actual hardware. This paper introduces a novel approach for automated system call filtering in
containerized applications. Typically, interactive applications within
containers engage in system calls that may compromise security and pose risks
to system stability. Existing methods for system call filtering rely on pre-
configured policies, often failing to account for the dynamic nature of modern
microservice applications. In response, we present a method for an intelligent
agent to independently discover and define system call policies for such
applications. The agent uses a machine learning technique, called Active
Learning, to identify and learn from unknown system calls made by the
application. Moreover, the agent develops a temporal framework to manage these
discoveries and ensure consistency across multiple instances of the application.
Our approach is successfully demonstrated through experiments using the Apache
Kafka and Elasticsearch applications. Further details about our research can be
found on our website: https://gruppe6.github.io/Timeloops/. Evaluations and
open-source code are accessible at: https://github.com/gruppe6/Timeloops. This
research was funded by RCN project number 270566. An earlier version of this
work was presented at ACM SIGSAC 2022. This paper has been accepted for
publication in a special issue of ACM Transactions on Security.

The practical effectiveness of linear classifiers largely hinges on efficient algorithms for determining their optimal separating hyperplanes. In the context of real-valued features, this is straightforward and well-established. However, for variables taking on values within a certain range, more nuanced approaches are needed to identify the optimal separating planes. We contribute to filling this knowledge gap by developing a general method for finding the optimal separating planes in various commodity spaces. We then apply this method to develop efficient algorithms for training linear classifiers in these spaces. By employing basic transformations, we demonstrate how linear classifiers can be trained in spaces with integer-valued, modular, and vector-valued variables. We then evaluate our algorithms through experiments involving training models on datasets featuring integer, binary, and list-valued labels. We also illustrate their utility in tasks such as data segmentation and approximate $k$-means clustering. Furthermore, we provide theoretical guarantees for the performance of these algorithms in terms of their worst-case and average-case errors. We then verify these bounds through experiments and compare the performance of our algorithms with respect to their runtime. We found that our methods consistently outperformed them significantly. Additionally, we employed microservices to evaluate the performance of our models on various datasets. We found that linear classifiers trained using our algorithms exhibited superior performance across a range of evaluation metrics, including accuracy and runtime. This paper presents a framework for compressive learning using the Independent Component Analysis (I CA) algorithm, enabling it to operate on under-determined data by incorporating sparse representation and learned dictionaries (LDA). We provide a detailed analysis of the effectiveness of sparse representation in facilitating identifiability and robust recovery in IC A, alongside the benefits of LDA in optimizing its performance. Building upon this understanding, we develop two novel algorithms: a dictionary learning method (CompI CA) and a hybrid algorithm (CompSP) that integrates sparse representation and LDA within the context of IC A. Through experimental evaluation, we showcase the capacity of these algorithms to learn identifiable dictionaries from sparse and noise-prone data, even in the absence of sparsity, thereby extending the applicability of IC A to compressed domains. In addition, we identify the optimal parameters for precise recovery and provide a quantitative metric for gauging the compressibility of IC A components. This research significantly expands the scope of IC A's applicability, enabling its use on datasets comprising numerous sources and compressed measurements. As such, it finds potential utility in various domains, including multi-band signal decoding and hyperspectral image processing. A range of hyperparameters govern the algorithms' behavior, and we thoroughly examine their impact to facilitate seamless integration into the algorithms. Through experimental evaluation, we showcase the algorithms' performance on diverse datasets, including synthetic data and real-world examples, such as decoding laser communications and hyperspectral image analysis. A range of hyperparameters, which we thoroughly investigate, notably the LDA's learning rate and the CompSP's step size, significantly affect the algorithms' behavior, as we clearly demonstrate. Furthermore, we extensively evaluate and discuss the performance metrics for assessing component compressibility, including the sparse-signal-to-noise ratio (KSPSNR) and the mean square error (MSE) with and without sparse representation. This quantitative assessment enables optimal parameter selection for precise recovery and accurately estimate the number of sources (K) from compressed data. We aim to achieve our goals through a series of workshops, as well as the development of educational content and outreach programs, particularly targeting primary and secondary education levels. The effectiveness of using a programmable phase disc to correct spherical and chromatic aberrations in the transmission electron microscope (TEM) was investigated through numerical simulations of imaging a 2 nm fine feature. By treating the phase disc as a quasi-object plane, we employed scalar wave optics principles to simulate how it corrects aberrations and enhance imaging performance. Our findings can inform the design of such a phase disc for utilization within an existing or modified TEM setup. Although the phase disc can improve imaging, our results indicate that its application is feasible only within a limited range of electron energies and is not practical for low-energy observations due to excessive shadowing effects. Recent advances in text-to-speech systems have achieved significant improvements.
However, naturally occurring conversations depart from standard speech norms.
A key challenge is producing speech that accounts for the complexities and variations of dialogue contexts.
To address this, a novel approach incorporating masking techniques is proposed within a continuous speech synthesis framework.
By segregating spoken words into background and foreground categories, distinct synthesis models can be applied to each.
Context-specific prosody modeling is also employed to enhance coherence across the entire dialogue.
Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses existing high-quality TTS systems in terms of conversational effectiveness. 
Related code and data can be accessed via the repository: https://github.com/zhousf123/MaskedDialogue.

A machine learning model's reliability relies heavily on data integrity, and any manipulation of its input can result in incorrect class predictions, offering potential benefits to attackers. Research into manipulating ML models through adversarial examples has focused on robustness against precise attacks, but this work reveals that only a few crafted examples can severely damage an model's accuracy. While existing studies on adversarial examples examine instances that affect a single target class, our investigation uncovers a more insidious threat: a person-in-the-middle (MitM) attack that can be launched using a small number of crafted examples that simultaneously affect multiple classes. This attack can be carried out by individuals with access to the data creation process or networks transporting the information. Furthermore, this work reveals that utilizing malicious generative frameworks can enable attackers to create multiple examples simultaneously, and confirms that only a few examples can compromise an model's reliability. To address this threat, our research introduces novel metrics for evaluating ML model robustness against person-in-the-middle attacks, and proposes a new framework for detecting and mitigating such attacks. This work executes its investigation on popular image classification models, but this type of attack can potentially be applied to other domains. The research also reveals that utilizing generative models can enable attackers to expand an model's training dataset with malicious examples, resulting in an increased attack impact when the model encounters new data. This reveals a new area of research and it can be seen that person-in-the-middle attacks offer a realistic threat to machine learning models deployed in various settings. The research provides a first-of-its-kind evaluation on the impact of such attacks, and it can be seen that person-in-the-middle attacks offer a more potent threat compared to existing adversarial examples. The research introduces novel metrics for evaluating machine learning robustness against such attacks, and it can be seen that only a few examples can severely damage an model's accuracy. The research also reveals that person-in-the-middle attacks can be carried out by individuals with access to data transport networks, making them a more realistic threat compared to existing adversarial examples. Climate change denials spread rapidly through online networks, often wrapped in conspiracy theories that evolve over time. Despite concurrent emergence in mainstream media circles, these theories exhibit distinct online lifecycles. This paper presents three unclassified examples of climate change conspiracy theories currently circulating: one that emerged in the 1990s, another that gained traction in the 2000s, and a relatively recent variant. Analyzing almost 19 million social media posts, our findings reveal that climate change conspiracy theories are increasingly popular, especially those promoted by high-reach online accounts. Moreover, these theories show a distinct seasonal pattern in online prevalence, mirroring the pattern of varying temperature readings in temperate climates. This suggests a possible link between climate change-related misinformation and temperature fluctuations. The coexistence of different conspiracy theory versions also correlates with distinct online events, including news headlines and polarizing politics. Understanding the dissemination of climate change conspiracy theories across social media platforms could enable the development of timely and targeted strategies to counteract their spread. Moreover, recognizing the online lifecycle of these theories may facilitate anticipation of future variants and adaptations. Finally, acknowledging the connection between temperature readings and online prevalence of conspiracy theories could foster collaborative efforts between technology companies and environmental organizations to address the spreading misinformation and promote climate awareness. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/jjindal9 ClimateAltTheory. The dataset can be obtained by contacting the corresponding author at pdevy@umd.edu. The social media data used in this research was collected using the Twitter API, with a data sampling rate of 50% to adhere to API restrictions and maintain comprehensive results. The Twitter sample comprises 44,844,772 tweets and 9,697,771 unique authors. The dataset also includes news articles from Kaggle, comprising 1,929,511 entries. News headlines were filtered to focus on climate change-related conspiracy theories, as well as unrelated topics to compare and distinguish the conspiracy theories from standard news coverage. The climate change-related conspiracy theory variants were selected based on prior research, including I. Climate change is a hoax, II. Climate change is beneficial, III. Climate change is natural, IV. Climate change is impending, and V. Climate change is a plot by geo-engineers. The selected theories encompassed the full spectrum of conspiracy theories and ensured that the research results would be representative and generalizable. The data was then analyzed using the Jaccard similarity index to calculate the similarity between different conspiracy theory variants and online prevalence patterns. Theoretical models propose the existence of shadow matter, feeble interactions with ordinary matter, as a form of dark matter. In a search for shadow matter using data from 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC, equations involving cross-sections of extra particles were developed. Analyzing the momentum distribution of extra particles and their alleged counterparts, either individually or in pairs, revealed no statistically significant deviations from expected values. In a specific scenario with a single top quark involved, a limit of 61 TeV was set on the scale of shadow matter, while the limits for the scenario with a top quark duo were between 58 and 82 TeV. These measurements represent the first practical application of the theoretical concept of shadow matter in physical experiments. In a top quark duo analysis, the theoretical concept of shadow matter was shown to be effective in a model with a 3-partita shadow matter duo, resulting in a limit of 261 TeV for this specific model. Furthermore, these measurements have set the stage for future searches for shadow matter in a wide range of physical processes at the upcoming HL-LHC. Additionally, these searches for shadow matter also involve evaluating how well Equations (2)-(4) can predict the momentum distribution of extra particles from the start, offering a method for verifying these equations in experiments and further developing the theoretical understanding of shadow matter. Finally, these searches for shadow matter have also revealed an anomaly in the theoretical model using Equations (2)-(4), which will be investigated further in the future. The anomaly is primarily due to the difference between the predicted and actual cross-sections at low scales, which needs to be reconciled. The possible sources of anomaly are due to the model using Equations (2)-(4) not fully taking into account the physical interactions between shadow matter and ordinary matter, which might be addressed by introducing additional equations into the model. The anomaly is present in the theoretical shadow matter model using a single top quark and a top quark duo, both of which need to be investigated further. The future searches for shadow matter at the HL-LHC will focus on fully incorporating the physical interactions between shadow matter and ordinary matter, which will likely result in a better fit between the predicted and actual cross-sections. The theoretical understanding of shadow matter, particularly through the model using Equations (2)-(4), offers a valuable method for studying its properties, which might be accomplished by looking into the decay products of extra particles and their alleged counterparts

We've developed three new cosmological theories, which we call the fluctuation-based, rarefaction, and compression theories. These theories explain the observed flatness of the universe in a unified manner. Specifically, the theories state that certain aspects of the universe are constantly smooth because they're governed by invariant average values during expansion. The theories work by applying statistical principles to a lattice representing space. We've demonstrated that the theories result in a flat universe through both analytical and numerical calculations. Additionally, we've shown that the theories naturally lead to a flat universe by regulating certain parameters within a limited range. The theories also predict that certain key cosmological quantities will follow power-law patterns as the universe ages. We've verified these predictions through numerical simulations. Ultimately, the theories provide a potential framework for understanding the universe's evolution while controlling variability. However, we've also identified potential challenges to incorporating the theories into a complete theoretical framework. We've calculated the number of independent parameters required to describe the universe's dynamics and found that the resulting number lacks clarity. We recommend further study to elucidate the universe's parameters and to explore the possibility of a phase transition that may have occurred during the universe's early stages. We've also conducted a preliminary analysis of how the theories apply to the observed distribution of galaxy spin in the universe. The outcome is encouraging, as the models based on the theories match the observed distribution relatively well, particularly when considering the spectrum's overall shape. However, we've also found that the galaxies' maximum rotational velocity does not follow the observed inverse distance relationship, at least within a certain range. The discrepancy may be attributed to a non-uniform distribution of galaxies that reflects their non-random movement. The underlying assumption of the theories that the galaxies are statistically uniformly distributed throughout space may be too limited to fully explain the observed galaxy dynamics. The most pressing question is whether the theories can provide a comprehensive explanation for the universe's observed structure and it's many intricate details, or if the key to understanding the universe lies in incorporating non-uniform patterns and movements into the existing theoretical framework. The numerical simulations reveal that the theories result in a smooth and flat universe, but they also highlight the need to consider the universe's inherent non-uniformity as a key factor in understanding its dynamics. The task of image partitioning aims to divide a given image into distinct regions based on specific characteristics, and this field has practical applications in image segmentation, object recognition, image compression, and image retrieval. A novel model, referred to as the Image Partitioning Variational Model (IPVM), is introduced in this study to accomplish image partitioning while also utilizing reconstructed image features to improve results. To achieve this, IPVM incorporates a spatially-adjacent cost function into the model, allowing for the division of images into meaningful and contiguous regions. An alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm is developed to solve the IPVM problem, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of multiple experiments utilizing datasets consisting of natural images and synthetic images with known regions of interest (ROIs). Our findings reveal that the proposed IPVM method outperforms baseline approaches in image partitioning tasks. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of reconstructed image features on the quality of partitioning results, and the significance of this investigation lies in the limited research that has previously addressed this topic. Our results indicate that the incorporation of reconstructed image features can enhance the quality of partitioning results, particularly in scenarios where images undergo degradation in the form of blurriness or corruption. The proposed IPVM model, coupled with the reconstructed features, has the potential to be applied to a wide range of real-world image partitioning tasks that involve degraded or noisy images. The source code for this model has been made available for public access at https://github.com/cvux/IPVM.git. Furthermore, the reconstructed image features can be utilized for image enhancement purposes, and the performance of the reconstructed images has been evaluated using numerical metrics, such as the multi-scale structural similarity index and peak signal-to-noise ratio. The average time required to solve the IPVM problem for an image of size $512 \times 512$ was approximately $152$ seconds, and the model exhibited consistency and robustness through repeated experiments. The proposed IPVM method has been demonstrated to be versatile and can be applied to images of various colors and sizes. However, it is worth noting that the model may experience increased computational costs for larger image sizes. The study presents a novel approach to image partitioning that incorporates reconstructed image features and utilizes a spatially-adjacent cost function, and the proposed model represents a novel addition to the field of image partitioning. IEEE 802.11p is widely utilized for vehicular communications, as it supports reliable access to road-related information. Short path loss, resulting from a vehicle's movement, poses a significant challenge for maintaining accurate 802.11p signal strength predictions. Existing methods have demonstrated some capability in addressing this issue, yet they fail to fully capture the dynamics of 802.11p channel variations. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel LSTM-based channel estimation framework that incorporates past measurement data into the current estimation model. By utilizing real-world data from an instrumented road segment, we show that our proposed method is capable of producing more accurate predictions and outperforming various baseline methods. Furthermore, we investigate and discuss the impact of several critical parameters on the performance of our LSTM-based estimator. To evaluate the predictive capabilities of our model, we extend it to forecast short-term 802.11p channel variations up to 50 ms into the future. Our experimental results confirm that leveraging past data in an LSTM-based framework leads to significantly improved forecasting accuracy. While increasing the sampling period of our LSTM model affects future prediction accuracy, our evaluations indicate that our model remains robust to period variations. Consequently, our proposed LSTM-based framework presents a effective solution for short-term 802.11p channel estimation. To facilitate reproduction of our results by other researchers, our source code for the IEEE 802.11p channel generator and LSTM-based estimator is freely available online at a public GitHub repository. Additionally, instrumented data collected from our road testing are also freely available at a public GitHub repository for the benefit of other researchers. To address the shortness of our collected test data, we apply time series techniques to generate synthetic data and evaluate the performance of our proposed LSTM model on both actual and artificially extended datasets. Our findings indicate that our LSTM-based estimator remains accurate when trained using synthetic data, as it is primarily influenced by the underlying vehicular road conditions rather than the specific characteristics of the data. Consequently, our proposed time-smoothing LSTM-based channel estimation method presents a effective, scalable, and data-independent solution for IEEE 802.11p channel estimation. The task of relation extraction aims to extract meaningful relationships between entities within a given text. Traditional approaches to this task rely on classification models that link entities to predefined relationship categories. To improve the accuracy of relation extraction, researchers have integrated knowledge graph enhancement, a technique which utilizes existing relationship information in the graph to inform text-based predictions. Building upon this approach, we present a novel method that leverages knowledge graph link prediction to guide entity classification in relation extraction. This method involves treating the relation extraction task as a collective inference problem and utilizing a graph attention mechanism to aggregate information from multiple entities. By applying this approach, we achieved state-of-the-art results on the ITSW dataset, matching the accuracy of existing one-stage models while operating at a significantly faster processing speed. Furthermore, we discovered that our method can successfully incorporate knowledge graph enhancement using techniques such as KonceptNet. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we performed ablation studies on various graph enhancement methods and found that they consistently improve the model's performance. To facilitate the use of this approach in real-world scenarios, we also developed a simple framework for selecting the most relevant entities from a given text based on their associated node features. To demonstrate the efficacy of this method, we performed a case study using the MedLine dataset, which showed that it yields a 5% improvement in accuracy over a baseline model that treats entity selection and classification as separate tasks. The code for this method is available on GitHub.

In cases of unanticipated changes in unknown conditions, machine learning models are required to adapt based on a limited number of samples obtained from the shifted environment. This work presents a novel approach to deal with such unsupervised domain adaptation problems where predictive models are expected to perform accurately on a new dataset with unknown background noises. Our strategy involves utilizing two types of labels - cause and effect - to create synthetic training data, thereby forming a semi-generative model. This semi-generative model is hybridized with a non-parametric technique to create a conditional generator that helps eliminate background noise present in the new dataset. Our method is demonstrated to be effective through empirical tests in various domains, such as image and text domains, where it is compared with other cutting-edge methods and shown to yield superior performance in multiple scenarios. The source code for our proposed method is available at https://github.com/jbavillier/SEM. Additionally, a demonstration of this work is uploaded to the following location: https://sem-badges.herokuapp.com/. Our theoretical framework has implications that extend beyond domain adaptation, suggesting the potential for background noise to impact the accuracy of synthetic sampling-based models, with further investigation warranted. The sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations poses a significant challenge in studying fermionic systems, particularly those exhibiting quantum spin liquids and superconductivity. A novel method using complex-valued neural networks to transform weighted data and mitigate the sign problem has been developed. This method, tested on the fermionic Hubbard model, demonstrates the ability to obtain accurate physical results even with a large number of weighted data points, and its efficiency improves as the model size increases. Additionally, we find that using rotation-inspired complex-valued neural networks results in more effective sign transformation and ground state prediction compared to their real-valued counterparts. Further applications of this method are proposed to study complex fermionic systems. \\
