Our understanding of how our brains process information from multiple sources in a 3D environment is essential for creating immersive virtual reality experiences. The technique of head-mounted light-weight VR systems typically relies on two-dimensional displays and stereoscopic vision to replicate a three-dimensional perception similar to real-world conditions. However, the limitations of these systems can result in discrepancies between the sensory information and physical environment, which can lead to perceptual alterations. In this paper, we explore the possibility of introducing temporal variations in the temporal coherence of sensory information, which enables the identification of the shadow aspect of perceptual alterations. The findings of our research demonstrate the presence of perceptual alterations with varying temporal frequencies, which can potentially be employed for the development of novel interactive applications that utilize sensory information. In particular, we discovered that high-frequency variations are observable under diminished lighting conditions and are characterized by distorted shapes, whereas low-frequency variations are independent of lighting conditions and are identified as shadows. The employment of high-resolution motion parallax can serve as a criterion for distinguishing between 2D and 3D perceptual alterations. Additionally, high-frequency high-resolution motion parallax can be employed in the design of interactive applications that utilize sensory information in line with real-world conditions. Lastly, our research provides a sensory-stream approach that prioritizes the preservation of high-frequency information in the development of interactive sensory algorithms to maintain consistency with real-world conditions. The data collected from our research experiments are available online. Future research can build upon our findings, such as examining the underlying mechanisms of the shadow aspect, extending our research to audio modalities, or designing interactive applications that utilize high-frequency information based on temporal variations of sensory coherency. In that context, we hope to demonstrate that high-frequency information can be harnessed for the creation of immersive VR experiences that exceed the limitations of current head-mounted display technology. To assess various approaches to expanding a multilingual model to new languages, 
we evaluate nine distinct methodologies for introducing eight previously unseen 
languages into the renowned BigScience multilingual framework. 
The evaluation criteria focus on the ability of the model to understand sentences 
in these new languages and its ability to generate coherent text in them. 
The efficacy of these approaches is tested using three different metrics and 
repeated with eight newly added languages, subject to three different training 
configurations to account for the impact of training data. 
The results show that certain methods are exceptionally effective in achieving 
good performance on new languages with minimal impact on the original ones. 
A novel technique involving the fine-tuning of the model's internal word 
embodiments on monolingual datasets proves particularly effective in boosting 
performance on unseen languages, highlighting the significance of the model's 
internal structure in its functionality. 
Additionally, we observe that the length of the new language's words typically 
falls within the range of the three to seven characters, while its vocabulary 
size is generally in the range of the two to the three thousand words. 
Based on these findings, a straightforward word-splitting approach can be 
employed to effectively understand sentences in these new languages. 
Regarding text generation, a straightforward yet reliable approach involving 
the repetition of words can be achieved under the condition that the model's 
internal structure is adequately understood. 
Consequently, a unified model framework can be employed to effectively 
accommodate a diverse range of new languages across various dimensions. 
The full code for replicating our results is publicly available on GitHub. 
Our research presents a comprehensive study on the expansion of the BigScience 
multilingual model to new languages, promoting its further development and 
evaluation through systematic assessments.

platform, facilitating the scalable distribution of our dataset, comprising 
eight newly added languages and approximately 13 million training samples.

three example categories - "seen", "unseen long", and "unseen short" - with 
respect to word length.

while "unseen long" and "unseen short" denote Italian and Serbian, respectively. 
The model's understanding and text generation capabilities in these scenarios

We establish that the collection of domains with the $\sigma$-elementary property exhibits vast variability. To substantiate this, we demonstrate the existence of a limitless number of distinct domain families, each of which possesses the $\sigma$-elementary characteristic. In particular, we identify a countless number of domains that can be represented using the normalization of Gerono's tetration sequence, $\mathop{\rm Nor}_{\!N}(\sigma)$ for a given natural number $N \ge 2$. These domains are $\sigma$-elementary and cannot be expressed as a pointwise extension of the $\sigma$-elementary domain $\mathbb{C}$, nor can their domains be composed from each other via the $\sigma$-extension operation. We show that the domains characterized by $\mathop{\rm Nor}_{\!N}(\sigma)$ have unique properties and that the function $\mathop{\rm Nor}_{\!N}(z)$ is continuous on the entire complex plane. We also prove that the domain $\mathbb{C}$ can be represented as a finite union of countably infinite subsets for each $N \ge 2$, thereby providing an infinite number of distinct domain families, each of which is $\sigma$-elementary. Additionally, we propose a method for defining fractal domains using the normalization of the $\sigma$-iteration sequence, $\mathop{\rm Nor}_{\!\mathfrak{p}}(\sigma)$, for a probability measure $\mathfrak{p}$ on the set $\{2, 3, \ldots, \infty\}$, thereby expanding our previous findings and illustrating the abundance of $\sigma$-elementary domains with unique properties. We also examine the relationship between the fractal dimension of domains characterized by $\mathop{\rm Nor}_{\!\mathfrak{p}}(\sigma)$ and the probability $\mathfrak{p}$ associated with its support set. We further investigate the connection between the fractal dimension of these domains and the fractal dimension of their images under the $\sigma$-mapping, while also looking into the geometric characteristics of domain images and variations in their fractal dimensions as $\mathfrak{p}$ changes. We also show that the fractal dimension of the domain $\mathbb{C}$, which is a pointwise extension of the $\sigma$-elementary domain, is unique and has a maximum value of $2$ on the entire complex plane. Verifying the integrity of program inputs typically involves an assertion language for specifying requirements and a mechanism for verifying those assertions. However, the process can be complicated by the fact that program inputs may not always be reliable, requiring assertions to be valid under both normal and adverse conditions. Despite this, the traditional approach to verification often treats the program's frame - the portion of its state that it doesn't modify - as a given, without considering what happens when it changes. This paper examines ways in which programs can be seen as exploring a framework, or pattern, of state, and uses this framework to redefine verification as a process of ensuring that program states remain consistent with this pattern, even in unpredictable situations. It also identifies a key challenge in this definition: accounting for program modifications, or how programs adapt to these changes. Overall, this paper provides a novel framework for understanding program modification and provides a method for defining and activating assertions that take into account a program's potential changes. It also identifies a program's mode, or state, as a key factor in this definition and explores its implications for verification. Ultimately, this work seeks to establish a universal method for defining and verifying program assertions, one that is based on the program's relationship to its state and is unaffected by external factors or special cases. To achieve this goal, this paper examines the program's behavior in various scenarios, including its mode and the program's control, or direction, to establish a method for defining and activating assertions, even in unpredictable situations. This result is contingent on a program's mode and control being compatible, a concept this paper terms 'program consistency.' Program consistency is a key concept in this study, representing a program's ability to be understood within the framework of its state. It is based on the program's mode and control and is essential for defining and verifying program assertions. This paper examines program consistency in various contexts, including its distribution over program states and the program's finite and infinite states. It also identifies a program with the property that its mode and control are never compatible, a so-called 'unconsistently' program. Additionally, this paper raises questions about when a program's mode and control are compatible and provides a method for defining program assertions based on this compatibility. It also identifies a program with the property that its mode and control are compatible only in certain situations, a so-called 'conditionally' program. A novel technique, known as the Distorting the CMB$\times$LSS method, has been created to quickly assess how non-Gaussian distortions affecting the cosmic microwave background's power spectrum and two-point cross-correlations with large-scale structure data could mislead our conclusions. Using a simplified approach based on a specific distortion type and two underlying cosmological models, the method generates simulated CMB and large-scale structure data that accurately matches the intended characteristics. It then compares the power spectrum and cross-correlation patterns in the simulated data with those of the original models, while also accounting for the effects of non-perturbative distortions on the CMB. As a demonstration of its utility, the Distorting the CMB$\times$LSS method has been used to investigate the impact of a simple distortion type on the results of a hypothetical large-scale structure data analysis, showing that significant changes can occur even if the cross-correlation spectrum remains unaffected. It has been further shown that, for a more realistic case involving more complex distortion types, the shape of the cross-correlation spectrum can provide valuable information that can help distinguish between different possible distortions, even when their values are similar. Therefore, while the presence of distortions may limit our understanding of the CMB, it is likely to have a much smaller effect on our conclusions regarding the properties of the early universe that are inferred from the cross-correlation spectrum, as well as those related to the growth of structure at late times. Nevertheless, current studies have primarily relied on non-verified assumptions, despite the fact that robustness can be verified in specific scenarios. We propose a new framework that integrates concepts from theoretical safety and machine learning, enabling the verification of robustness and improving learning outcomes on malicious datasets. The advantages of this framework become apparent when dealing with safety-critical applications, limited budget for training data, or when the impact of adversarial examples needs to be mitigated. The key to this framework is the utilization of a novel challenge model, designed in accordance with peer-to-peer adversarial learning paradigms, to simulate malicious manipulation, and a reliability measure that assesses the machine's performance under potential attacks. The machine's robustness can then be verified through precise risk assessment, and the optimal solution can be identified. A combination of diffusion models, namely, the independent and broadcast models, explains the behavior of rumor dissemination in China, with observations showing that this theory holds up in the country's Internet environment. To gauge the impact of misinformation, a metric based on the net diffusion radius is introduced, revealing that the damage from online rumors in China is relatively limited. Compared to critical medical information, the influence of misinformation on the public is relatively insignificant. However, the analysis further reveals that misinformation can still have an adverse impact on the public's mental health in ways that are difficult to measure numerically. To manage the spread of rumor misinformation, recommendations are made for both technology and media outlets to prioritize the blocking and dissemination of critical medical information. Furthermore, efforts to combat misinformation should prioritize understanding the specific context in which rumors are disseminated within China, rather than simply promoting general fact-checking initiatives. Remote sensing analysts use hyperspectral imaging, which involves spectral dimensionality reduction techniques to gather detailed spectral data, leading to vast amounts of spectral dimensionality data. This study investigates how different methods for dimensionality reduction, such as principal component analysis and self-taught learning, affect hyperspectral pixel classification. We examined six hyperspectral datasets from various environments, including urban, forest, agricultural areas, and deserts, and found that dimensionality reduction can both positively and negatively impact classification results. Notably, our findings suggest that dimensionality reduction can lead to improved classification rates in forest and urban settings, but detrimental effects in agricultural and desert scenarios. Overall, the outcomes highlight the importance of careful consideration and dataset-specific approaches when employing dimensionality reduction methods for hyperspectral pixel classification. Additionally, our results indicate that PCA is an suitable choice for forest classification but may not always be the best option for other settings. We also observed that employing HTL, a spectral uncorrelation method, can enhance the performance of classical PCA. We anticipate that our research will guide the selection of optimal spectral dimensionality reduction methods for various applications in hyperspectral imaging. A novel ensemble-based approach to predicting protein structures has emerged as a reliable method for confirming protein configurations. However, this approach's reliance on experimentally measured amide proton chemical shifts to refine conformational envelopes has been hindered by the limitations of current chemical shift prediction methods. We have developed a quantum-mechanics-based protocol for accurately predicting amide proton chemical shifts, and we demonstrate that incorporating these predictions into the ensemble calculation significantly improves the correlation between predicted and measured chemical shifts, thus facilitating the validation and refinement of protein structures. We illustrate the effectiveness of this method for the model proteins crambin and ubiquitin, and we discuss its potential application in refining experimentally determined protein structures. Additionally, we have made the quantum-mechanics-based chemical shift predictor code publicly available to aid in the development of next-generation protein structure refinement methods. We anticipate that this tool will be essential for advancing the ensemble approach to protein structure determination. Furthermore, we have introduced a novel criterion for assessing the reliability of predicted chemical shifts, and we have demonstrated its utility in evaluating the performance of prediction methods on datasets from a range of proteins. We believe that this criterion will be a valuable resource for researchers striving to achieve high levels of accuracy in chemical shift prediction, particularly when assessing results on proteins with unusual environmental conditions. Recent research in deep learning has demonstrated the potential of machine learning models to deliver highly accurate predictions in various classification tasks. Nevertheless, existing studies have mainly concentrated on the impact of different regularization techniques on model performance, while largely overlooking the significance of loss function modification. In this paper, we aim to bridge this knowledge gap by investigating the effect of loss function modification on binary and multiclass classification models. Our study compares the performance of multiple loss functions, including a modified loss function inspired by the global minimum variance risk, against the standard cross-entropy loss. Our findings indicate that loss function modification can yield superior performance in certain scenarios, highlighting the importance of careful model selection. Additionally, we demonstrate that combining different loss functions can facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of model performance and enable the identification of the optimal model hyperparameters through grid search. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub, allowing for replication of our results. Furthermore, we have released the GLF dataset, which can be utilized for future research in deep learning. Our study's source code and data can be accessed at the designated repository. forecasting and adaptive feedback in a learning system. Student forecasting
identifies likely areas of confusion among students, while adaptive feedback
provides tailored guidance to students who are predicted to be lost or struggling.

The objective of this research is to investigate how music's structural complexity has changed over time using sophisticated mathematical techniques. With the vast creation and dissemination of music across platforms like YouTube and Spotify, the traditional approach of analyzing physical recordings is insufficient. Thus, we've developed a data-driven method to study musical complexity that's applicable to large datasets. By analyzing a comprehensive music library spanning seven decades, we tested our method and observed a significant increase in musical complexity since the 1990s. Notably, the acceleration in musical complexity contradicts our initial expectations and those of previous studies. We've carefully examined the potential causes behind this trend, considering factors like style diversity, artistic freedom, and the influence of electronic music. Our findings suggest that the rise in musical complexity is largely attributed to the advent and popularity of electronic music. However, we've identified some indications of musical complexity reaching a plateau in recent years, which warrants further exploration. Ultimately, our research enables the development of a predictive model to estimate musical complexity based on genre-specific analysis. What does 'core-compact' refer to in this context?
In topology and domain theory, core-compact refers to a topological space having a specific property where for any two closed subsets of the space, their product space is homeomorphic to the closure of their image under the Kuratowski map. This is equivalent to the space being compactly generated if it has a compact topology or has a specific coverage that can be used to define a compact topology on the space itself. This is often denoted as a core-compact topological space or a core-compact point of a topological space. In the study at hand, core-compactness is examined within the context of a topological space's constructed domains such as Smyth and Eda powerdomains.

A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of being automatic and efficient in a Bayesian framework, it poses difficulties for implementing Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling due to the necessity of integrating out the process. To address these challenges, a new parameterization is proposed, one that reduces the dimensionality of the problem and enables efficient sampling. The proposed method is then evaluated on synthetic and real-world datasets. The predicted lifetime of the standard model Higgs boson decaying to a top quark and a strange quark is sensitive to new physics in the quark sector, and recent measurements have refined the estimate to 1 part in 100,000. In this review, I summarize the most accurate predictions of the predicted lifetime, specifically focusing on two models that incorporate flavor-changing neutral currents within the top quark interactions. By considering these models, scientists aim to understand why certain quark decays are permitted but remain unobserved, and these models offer potential explanations for this phenomenon, thus providing a means to detect potential issues with the predicted lifetime. In addition to these models, I also review predictions for decay rates involving supersymmetric neutral H+ and charmonium bose quarks. In the case of the LHCb experiment, scientists are working to refine the predicted estimates for the predicted lifetime, and our research aims to evaluate several theoretical models that can account for discrepancies in this measurement. Based on the current research, scientists expect to obtain an accuracy of around 10^-5 with 5.9 fb^-1 of data, and future updates with larger data sets will significantly reduce this error, enabling researchers to gain more insight into the potential impacts of new physics on this predicted measurement. In the case of the CMS experiment, scientists have successfully measured the predicted lifetime of the bottom quark, and our research aims to achieve a measurement with an error of around 10^-5 with 5.9 fb^-1 of data. Although the predicted error for this measurement appears to be 3*10^-5, scientists can refine this estimate by incorporating information from top quark pair events, and our research demonstrates that this goal is within reach, thus providing a means to further constrain the predicted quark parameters. To assess the transmission risk of viruses, such as influenza and SARS-CoV-2, we applied a mathematical framework to simulate an urban bus journey. By setting the initial conditions to include infected passengers, we measured the number of subsequent passenger infections. The outcome showed that under 'well-mixed' conditions, i.e., when passengers mix uniformly, a limited number of infections occurred among other passengers. Conversely, when passengers maintained social distancing by reducing face-to-face distances, the number of secondary infections among fellow passengers increased. Consequently, this suggests that maintaining a physical distance of at least 2 meters on urban buses can significantly reduce the transmission risk of viruses. Furthermore, our study demonstrated that relying solely on vaccine efficacy may be insufficient in preventing future outbreaks, as the critical percentage of individuals needing to be vaccinated to prevent an epidemic increases in proportion to the reduced physical distances among passengers. Therefore, we advocate for a multifaceted approach combining both vaccine efforts and social distancing measures to mitigate virus transmission effectively. The model parameters for our study, including the urban bus geometry and passenger movement patterns, are available for other researchers to use. Additionally, this approach enhances the performance of Deep Dynamic Neural Networks by creating a pre-processing step for reducing noise and improving data regularization.  Leveraging kernel learning allows LANDO to create a system structure from data, which we show can be effective in multiple applications.  Compared to current methods, LANDO detects nonlinear components more accurately and provides better performance in a wide range of scenarios. This research explores the process of an isolated neutron star capturing a nearby white dwarf through the atomic icing process, with emphasis on its implications for millisecond pulsar capture. Initially, a neutron star absorbs a white dwarf companion via tidal forces, ultimately incorporating its captured matter into its own core. Consequently, the captured white dwarf material solidifies into the pulsar's core, with the entire process unfolding over millions of years. Notably, this capture mechanism leaves behind a distinctive trail of lighter elements, predominantly consisting of silicon and oxygen, which could potentially be identified through stellar spectroscopic analysis. Furthermore, the characteristics of this capture event, including its duration and features, should align with those of supernovae Type IIb, with the displaced material from the neutron star surface evaporating to generate the pulsar wind, which in turn gives rise to the pulsar's magnetosphere. To investigate the radiated electromagnetic pulsar wind, this study involves one-dimensional numerical simulations of the pulsar's force balance, which yield estimates of its spin-down luminosity and luminosity radius. Additionally, the magnetosphere's edge density, radial temperature, and pressure are determined, with the edge density exhibiting a direct correlation with the capture event's duration. With the edge density varying by as much as six orders of magnitude, this research demonstrates that the density at the magnetosphere's edge can differ by several orders of magnitude, influenced greatly by the duration of the capture event. Consequently, the spin-down age of the pulsar is essentially dictated by the capture duration, thereby rendering the rotational slowdown frequency constant. Recent research has shown that virtual drawing skills can effectively predict 3D design creativity. However, freehand 3D sketches created in 2D spaces lack the inherent depth information necessary for retrieving exact 3D models. To bridge this gap, our approach proposes an innovative method for retrieving 3D models from virtual drawings with depth information. By projecting 3D surfaces onto 2.5D surfaces and aligning them with virtual drawings, we simulate the drawing process in 3D. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances retrieval accuracy compared to traditional methods. Future directions involve refining the deep learning-based framework and integrating multiple viewpoints to convey more complete spatial information. Our implementation and results can be accessed on our website. This research paves the way for a more realistic and effective 3D design inspired by traditional drafting techniques with depth perception. To demonstrate the potential, we also created a VR-based application that allows users to create 3D models from virtual drawings with depth information. This can be accessed at the provided URL. Our research contributes to bridging the limitation of 2D drawings in retrieving accurate 3D models and enables more realistic 3D design inspired by traditional drafting techniques with depth perception. A live demo is available at the provided URL.

HD80606b, a gas giant in the Kepler-10 system, undergoes extraordinary heat fluctuations due to its close proximity to its parent star. As the planet orbits around its star every 111.6 hours, it experiences extreme temperature changes of up to 800K during its monthly orbits. To make accurate observations of this phenomenon, especially with the launch of the James Webb Space Telescope, researchers need to make precise predictions of the planet's monthly orbits. Recent studies, including one by Madhusudhan et al. in 2011, used transit observations to propose a revised model for HD80606b's monthly orbits. However, the accuracy of this model needs further verification. To that end, a team of researchers conducted a worldwide telescope network observation of HD80606b, analyzing its effects on the parent star's brightness during its monthly orbits. Using appropriate theoretical models, the team analyzed the data from multiple telescopes and found that HD80606b's monthly orbits follow a particular pattern with an eccentricity of 0.016 +/- 0.005. Furthermore, the team also established the timing of the planet's closest approaches to its parent star, known as periastrons, which showed an earlier timing of 0.004 +/- 0.003 hours. As a result, the team proposed a revised model for the planet's monthly orbits that could improve the scheduling of the James Webb Space Telescope for observing HD80606b and similar planets. The periastron timing of the planet also showed potential implications for the planet's internal heat generation. Based on the team's analysis, it's possible that the internal heat generation of HD80606b could lead to its thermal contraction or expansion during its close proximity to its parent star, which might cause its orbital variability. The periastron of the planet occurred just 0.6 hours before its expected value, which could indicate that the planet is in a state of slight instability. A significant issue in robotics lies in achieving efficient motor learning for robots. The process of a robot mastering a new movement involves repeated attempts, but the current approach can be excessively time-consuming. Insights from human learning reveal that efficient learning is facilitated when the focus is on new and varied information. The contribution of end-effect outcomes, representing the final result of a movement, appears to be inconsistent in this context. In fact, focusing solely on these outcomes can hinder learning due to their relative infrequency. In contrast, focusing on the intermediate kinematic or dynamic factors seems more productive, albeit less feasible in terms of perception. The frequency of these factors is increased through manipulation, and their incorporation in the learning process yields improved efficiency. The proposal of an Investigation Drive, which prioritizes factors providing the most insight into the learning process, leads to enhanced learning speeds. The evaluation of this idea using simulated and real-world experiments demonstrates significant improvements in learning speeds, specifically an average increase of 3.3 times in cases where only end-effect outcomes were considered and up to 5.3 times in cases involving kinematic or dynamic factors. The practical application of this concept has been successfully tested on a UR5 robot using visual tracking of its movements to determine the relevant factors for efficient learning. The source code for the robot is publicly available, enabling others to replicate these findings. The findings of this study represent a meaningful contribution to the field, offering an efficient solution for robotic motor learning. Upward planarity is a rare phenomenon in graph theory, where a planar embedding can be transformed into an upward planar embedding by eliminating edges. This property is not only difficult to assess but also determining whether a graph lacks upward planarity is NP-complete. Our research introduces three algorithmic solutions to solve upward planarity assessments, each capable of efficiently processing complex graphs. The first method utilizes tractable constraints, exploiting cyclic sequence representations in upward embeddings. The second solution relies on parameterized logic and FPT algorithms, evaluating the impact of sequence constraints. The third algorithm combines sequence-based constraints with Buchsbaum et al.'s technique to assess upward planarity, finally proving that Delaunay triangulations of points in a 2-dimensional space can be solved within linear time. Our solutions yield linear-time algorithms for evaluating upward planarity in two specific graph types: planar duals and tree-exponential graphs, encompassing various notable graph classes as special cases. These results provide a comprehensive overview of upward planarity assessments, showcasing the efficiency of parameterized methods in graph theory. Our approaches can be adapted to evaluate monotone series, extending to upward planarity with outliers, which can be solved efficiently using an FFT-based algorithm. Our contribution significantly advances upward planarity assessments, exploiting sequence constraints and offering efficient algorithms for various graph types. The novel applications of the Brute Force Algorithm and the Challenging Component Algorithm introduce new perspectives for upward planarity assessments, while the FFT-based algorithm emerges as a promising solution for series with outliers. Ultimately, our solutions demonstrate the practical value of parameterized methods in graph theory, yielding efficient algorithms for complex graphs. Image-based recall is a fundamental concept in visual navigation.
However, current methods typically disregard the recall process, directly
using external pre-trained image features that fail to capture the rememberer's
perspective.
We propose a new recall mechanism, called MemoNav, that chooses relevant
images from a rememberer's perspective, using a view transformer to incorporate
agent pose information and a transformer encoder to prioritize forensically
relevant features.
In a practical recall scenario, MemoNav consistently outperforms other methods,
democratically performing equally well with both high and low quality observations.
Source code for this project is available at https://github.com/wcunzi/MemoNav.

Recent experiments aiming to understand the nature of the Hoyle state, a highly unstable nuclear state, have been attempted but have also been plagued by similar issues of interference from beta decay and molecular effects. To overcome these limitations, researchers have proposed using a Time-Proportional Counter, a detector system that can effectively eliminate beta decay's influence, allowing for a clearer assessment of the Hoyle state's properties. This proposal aims to tackle the long-standing question of whether the Hoyle state predominantly consists of a single, unified state or multiple overlapping states. Utilizing the capabilities of thinking-proportional counters to filter out beta decay, researchers can focus on the Hoyle state's primary characteristics, specifically its 0+ and 12+ resonance strengths, and thereby directly evaluate the Hoyle state's existence as a distinct state or a cluster gluon. This study will utilize data simulated using an IBS ring, integrated with a TPC, and processed with a machine learning-based analysis to determine the Hoyle state's properties. Results indicate that the Hoyle state's 0+ and 12+ resonance strengths agree with theoretical predictions, and its presence can be attributed to a single, distinct state, specifically a high-energy resonance state, namely the 4He hoyle state. Moreover, this experiment demonstrates that the predicted hoyle state strengths in 12C are significantly lower than earlier experiments using a magnetic spectrometer have suggested. Combining the present results with existing data, a medium- and model-averaged value of the 0+ and 12+ resonance strengths for the 12C hoyle state has been determined as 72(9) keV·mb, providing crucial insights into the nature of the hoyle state. Furthermore, this experiment shows that the predicted hoyle state strengths in 16O are substantially lower than earlier experiments using a magnetic spectrometer have suggested. The conditions that lead to the spontaneous creation of cracks in two-dimensional materials under stress are examined. This study finds that cracks form when the distance between an initial crack and a stress edge exceeds a certain threshold, which is determined by the material's inherent length scales. A second criterion indicates that cracks also form when the material's intrinsic time scales align with the stress oscillation periods. Intrinsic time scales develop due to large stresses that cause vibrational wobbles or tip-splitting instabilities. These findings are supported by simulations of two anti-phase materials subject to different stress patterns, including a linearly increasing stress and an alternating stress. The results show that different types of inherent length scales influence when cracks form in each scenario. Additionally, the existence of an inherent time scale prevents the occurrence of an unstable, self-propagating crack front. This research provides new insights into how materials respond to stress, particularly in situations where the stress waves interact with each other and the material's internal structures. These findings could potentially be applied to observe and measure crack behavior in experiments using sound waves or other forms of propagation. Such approaches may offer new perspectives on understanding fracture mechanics. Furthermore, this research could facilitate the development of advanced materials with controlled structures that can resist damage. By modeling specific types of inherent length scales, these studies could potentially be applied to both atomic arrangements and macroscopic features. Lastly, the studied mechanisms also exist in three-dimensional materials, which suggests that their applications could be even broader. This research paper introduces novel finite-conduit codes that incorporate feedback and state information at the encoder, complementing existing infinite conduit codes. Enabling the use of instantiations with discrete, finite memory, the proposed codes exploit knowledge about the encoder's internal state and receive feedback from the decoder. A specific example is provided by adding memory to the memoryless Gaussian feedback channel. Diverging from prior techniques that create infinite conduits, this work demonstrates that feedback and state information can be leveraged to develop conveyable codes with discrete memory. Such codes offer a means to transmit information over feedback channels with memoryless encoders, even with knowledge of the encoder's internal state and receive feedback. This allows for the transmission of information over channels with memory, utilizing the benefits of state information and feedback. As a result, the proposed codes can achieve rates surpassing those predicted by Shannon's information capacity, utilizing the benefits of state information and feedback. A corresponding decoding algorithm is also introduced, enabling optimal decoding of the proposed codes when the encoder's internal state is known. Furthermore, bounds on and approaches to the capacity are provided, enabling evaluation and assessment of the proposed codes. This complex system displays three distinct phases, which are characterized by pairings in spin and orbital components. Holographic quantum Hall phases emerge due to symmetry breaking in both spin and orbital parts, resulting in spin and orbital imbalances. Specifically, a spinful Fulde-Ferrell, a spinful Darboux-Popov and a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate can be observed, each with unique properties such as fractional orbital momentum quanta and phase patterns that are dependent on flux density. Experimental realization through optical lattice formation can potentially harness cold atom technology to observe these novel superfluid properties. This approach may also apply to modeling p-wave superconductors through an attractive Hubbard model. It also explores the effects of phase fluctuations within the topological regime, demonstrating that zero-energy two-component chiral Majorana edge modes can exist when supported by orbital pairing. Additionally, a stable spinful Fulde-Ferrell phase can be achieved when rational spin imbalance is applied, resulting in novel phenomena such as the potential for spinor mode generation. A recent study demonstrated that a significant portion of information in data tables is incorrect due to outdated data, misleading labels, or false data, which can cause severe consequences in various fields such as finance and medicine. To promote research in this area, SemEval 2021 introduced SEM-TAB-FACTS, a competition focused on verifying the accuracy of table data and identifying supporting evidence for truth verification. Participants were given four sub-table selection tasks and a fact verification task based on annotated tables from the PubMed database. Two sub-table classification tasks were also involved, requiring participants to find specific types of information or analyze tables with similar characteristics. Despite challenges posed by the pre-print dataset format and limited human annotations, participants demonstrated robust systems for table data verification and evidence searching, which showed promising potential for further development. A detailed examination of the results and system designs has been conducted, with participants' examples and explanations available online for reference. A future dataset will be made available for public use, comprising full annotations of approximately 15,000 tables, in addition to the current dataset with 1,421 annotated tables. It is anticipated that this dataset will facilitate research in multiple domains and contribute significantly to advancing the capabilities of automatic truth verification and evidence searching in tables. Word embedding-based models emerged as top performers in most categories, with notable exceptions including a top-ranked system that employed transformer architecture for fact verification and another that leveraged row embeddings for table classification. Additionally, several systems with similar architectures and features emerged close to the top in multiple sub-table selection tasks. Improvements were observed in all tasks, with particular gains in fact verification through the application of multi-head attention and convolutional neural networks. Notably, baseline models incorporating table embeddings proved ineffective in certain tasks, underperforming systems that relied on standard word embeddings. It was conjectured that the limited availability of human annotations may have impeded the effectiveness of models relying on table embeddings. A comparison of the top-ranked systems in fact verification and evidence searching across sub-tables revealed that their performances varied significantly with the number of columns in tables, with many struggling to achieve satisfactory accuracy in tables possessing eight or more columns. Consequently, developing systems capable of dealing with diverse table structures from the targeted domain appears essential. This paper delves into the concept of complex numbers within quantum physics, presenting both its historical development and current applications. It highlights the success of complex numbers in quantum mechanics and their continued utilization in quantum field theory. Additionally, the paper discusses how complex numbers remain essential for contemporary research in both particles and fields. However, the author also acknowledges the long-standing debates surrounding their necessity, referencing specific criticisms from the schools of de Broglie and Bohm. To resolve this concern, the author proposes a novel argument, suggesting that even if one chooses to work with real wavefunctions over complex ones, the phase space can still be represented through real-valued pairs, thereby preserving the essential properties of quantum states. Nevertheless, the author takes a contrarian view, asserting that quantum physics inherently requires complex numbers, albeit without dismissing the validity of Bohmian mechanics as a potential interpretation. Ultimately, the paper concludes by noting notable researchers who have expressed skepticism towards the use of complex numbers, with a hope that this perspective may spark further discussion. Note that this perspective presents the author's individual viewpoint and may not reflect a unified stance of Cambridge University. A graph G is considered fully measurable if every vertex v of G has a unique path leading to every other vertex in the graph. The minimum number of vertices required for full measurability is known as the graph's metric dimension and can be found through an optimal set of vertices known as an independent set of witnesses. A faster version of this concept, known as shortened metric dimension, involves using fewer vertices while maintaining full measurability for certain graph types. Specifically, it's achievable with n/2 vertices for even graph sizes n and specifically 3n/4 for fully connected graphs. This result also extends to certain graph classes where a lower bound of n/2 can still be found. The idea of shortened metric dimension provides a limited but efficient solution to full measurability, allowing it to be applied to certain graph classification problems. Notably, it's possible to determine in polynomial time whether a given independent set of witnesses exists in an n vertex graph, and also to find such a set with a modified metric dimension of n/2 in the same amount of time. These findings also hold for fully connected graphs and certain graph classification problems where a lower bound of n/2 can still be found. soil and its boundaries. We consider fluids as substances with inherent
property variations depending on the relative position of their molecules, 
and apply this perspective to fluids within soil and atmospheric pressure 
conditions. By examining the force balance on a soil volume, we derive a 
partial differential equation describing the slow movement of fluids and 
pumps within the soil. Assuming hydraulic head uniform across soil 
boundaries, this equation simplifies to Phillips, Neumann, and Boussinesq 
equations for groundwater flow. We also address the challenge of predicting

This research introduces an innovative method to efficiently remove sulfur dioxide (SOx) from flue gas through a chemical oxidation process using ozone (O3) and ultraviolet (UV) light. The study identifies the optimal O3/UV ratios for achieving SOx elimination reactions and reveals that increasing UV intensity enhances O3 consumption, yet reduces energy costs. A merged O3/UV merger model is developed to analyze the combined effects of O3 and UV on the oxidation process, and the results indicate that a higher O3 injection rate can compensate for UV intensity fluctuations and maintain stable SOx elimination performance. Moreover, the study evaluates the energy and economic feasibility of the proposed system and demonstrates that integrating UV light into the O3 oxidation process can decrease energy consumption by 63% compared to a system using only O3. The research further examines the technical viability of the merged O3/UV system and shows that integrating UV light reduces the required O3 injection rate by 50%, extending its operational lifespan and thereby improving the technology's overall cost-effectiveness. The research ultimately identifies the influences of UV light emission spectra, O3 injection location, and gas mixing patterns on the performance of the merged system, providing valuable insights for system design and optimization. The findings largely conform to the predictions made by the merged O3/UV model, demonstrating excellent accuracy. The research does, however, acknowledge some discrepancies between simulated and experimental results, which are investigated, for the most part, as instrumentation errors. The study concludes by highlighting the promising features of the merged O3/UV system and recommending further research into its integration with other flue gas treatment technologies to create a unified, energy-efficient system for the elimination of SOx. The merged O3/UV process is expected to play a significant role in the development of future low-cost, large-scale flue gas desulfurization technology. Current commercial simulators for neuromorphic hardware have several limitations, 
primarily due to their focus on specific architecture types and lack of advanced 
features such as mixed-mode cosimulation with digital and analog components. 
To address these shortcomings, we have developed a new, based-on-SystemC framework 
that allows for the development of complex applications involving large-scale 
spiking neural networks. Additionally, this framework can efficiently simulate 
component-level models of stateful digital circuits that interact with analog 
circuits. Furthermore, it provides a concurrent simulation mode and supports 
hardware-in-the-loop testing for verifying continued functionality after mapping 
neuromorphic applications onto actual neuromorphic chips. Our framework offers a 
useful tool for both software designers and hardware architects to evaluate and 
optimize various design choices for neuromorphic systems before bringing them to 
bear on real-world problems. As proof of concept, we have successfully mapped 
spiking neural network models onto both a previously developed GDC chip and the 
PYNQ-ZYNQ-7030 FPGA, using the proposed framework to guide the mapping process. 
Based on these experiments, we have achieved significant reductions in energy 
consumption by selecting the most critical neurons for placement on the GDC 
chip while prioritizing the remaining neurons on the FPGA. As a result, we have 
obtained an energy savings of approximately 65% at the expense of increased 
latency. Our study also reveals that the current GDC chip falls short of ideal 
performance due to its outdated architecture; however, we have identified several 
design choices and potential workarounds that could further enhance energy 
efficiency. Finally, we have verified the accuracy of our model by comparing it 
to actual hardware results and observed minimal simulation errors of less than 1%. 
Overall, our framework facilitates fast, thorough simulations of neuromorphic 
systems, paving the way for further optimizations. Furthermore, it enables 
the rapid development of realistic benchmark applications, thus enabling more 
precise evaluations of various architecture types and design choices. Given its 
based-on-SystemC architecture, our framework is highly adaptable and can be 
customized to support a broad range of simulation modes and hardware platforms.

Machine learning algorithms are frequently employed for systems with subtle decision-making processes, often incorporating uncertain or disputed data in their models, even when these models themselves are uncertain about the relevance of such information. Current learning algorithms are generally able to handle single instances of uncertainty, but fail in cases where there are multiple, interconnected ambiguities. This work introduces a novel learning setting to address models that incorporate multiple, interconnected uncertainties. We also develop a corresponding algorithm, Forest of \emph{Or}, and demonstrate its efficacy through experiments involving cases that take into account the full spectrum of possible uncertainties, such as (i) decision-making processes that ignore irrelevant information, (ii) processes that incorporate all information, but with degrees of ambiguity, and (iii) processes that prioritize specific information categories. Our results show that Forest of \emph{Or} performs exceptionally well across all scenarios, even when there are multiple, interconnected uncertainties, and that it can often match or outperform models that have complete information about relevant categories. Notably, Forest of \emph{Or} has the ability to automatically discover and utilize key information categories, and even extends to a version of popular algorithm Random Forest when there is a single, overarching ambiguity. The PrunedDTW algorithm represents a optimized version of the DTW template alignment, allowing for significant time reductions while maintaining equivalent results. By enforcing the pruned constraint from the start of the comparison and discarding off-limits data, PrunedDTW achieves a time complexity of O(n^2), substantially improving upon DTW's O(n^3) performance. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW still exhibits sub-optimal real-time capabilities due to its quadratic complexity. In this study, we propose a modified variant, referred to as Early Discarding PrunedDTW (EDPrunedDTW), which enhances the pruned constraint to include previously unbounded data, thereby increasing the searchable interval and potentially allowing for early discarding of data. By doing so, EDPrunedDTW attains a linear time complexity under fixed error thresholds. Our evaluations, conducted using various datasets of time series, demonstrate that EDPrunedDTW significantly boosts the percentage of early discarding opportunities, thereby reducing computation time. Moreover, we demonstrate the potential applications of EDPrunedDTW in similarity retrieval tasks. Our source code is freely accessible via GitHub. We anticipate that EDPrunedDTW will serve as an efficient early discarding strategy, providing a solid foundation for future research in efficient DTW-based retrieval methods. Additionally, we have introduced a simplified early discarding variant, referred to as Simple PrunedDTW (SpPrunedDTW), which is likely to be a more accessible and robust algorithm than PrunedDTW and could serve as a useful baseline in future studies. Our source code for SpPrunedDTW is also freely available via GitHub. We anticipate that SpPrunedDTW will serve as an efficient early discarding strategy, providing a simple and robust foundation for future research in efficient DTW-based retrieval methods. Furthermore, we have proposed a generalised early discarding variant, referred to as Generalised PrunedDTW (GPrunedDTW), which is likely to be a more efficient and versatile algorithm than PrunedDTW and could serve as a thorough foundation for future research in efficient DTW-based retrieval methods. Our source code for GPrunedDTW is also freely accessible via GitHub. We anticipate that GPrunedDTW will distinguish itself from other early discarding approaches through its extensive theoretical justification. We introduce a novel perspective on graph convolutional networks' output
smoothness, which leads to the Graph Convolutional Network Smoothing Problem
(GCNSP). To address this problem, we develop a metric to quantify the
smoothness of graph convolutional networks. This metric proves useful in
two actual tasks: (1) enhancing node feature generation quality and (2) extending
the scope of over-smoothing theory from fixed-width networks to variable
dimensional graphs. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. 

Notably, we found that the graph convolutional network's output smoothness
is largely unaffected by the number of layers, but heavily influenced by the
size of the output vector. As a result, a larger output vector size leads to
a lower metric value, indicating reduced output smoothness. Our results also
show that the proposed metric provides a reliable indicator of the graph
classification accuracy. This means that graphs classified efficiently tend
to have a lower metric value. We also observed that the proposed metric can
be utilized as a stopping criterion for training graph convolutional networks
by monitoring the training node classification accuracy and the metric value. 

To validate the generalizability of the proposed metric, we tested it on
different datasets and found a positive correlation between the metric value
and the graph classification accuracy. The influence of the graph structure
on the metric value was also examined, with our findings indicating that
the graph classification accuracy is highly correlated with the metric value
for distinct graphs. The code for our approach is available on GitHub. 

This research builds on the graph convolutional network's ability to apply
nearest-neighbor based interpolation to generate output features. We also
derive an expression for the graph convolutional network's Lipschitz constant
and establish a relationship between the constant and the metric value. 

In particular, we found that the graph convolutional network's Lipschitz
constant is directly proportional to the maximum eigenvalue of the graph
structure. The graph convolutional network's ability to apply nearest-neighbor
based interpolation leads to its output features being influenced by the
graph's eigenvalues and eigenvectors. We also observed that the graph
classification accuracy is highly correlated with the graph's eigenvalues and
eigenvectors. Nonetheless, the graph classification accuracy is not directly
proportional to the graph's diameter. The graph convolutional network's
capacity to apply nearest-neighbor based interpolation also leads to its
output features being influenced by the graph's degree distribution

A comprehensive search for evidence of dark matter resulting from Z boson decay or associated particle production in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV was conducted using data collected by the CMS Collaboration in 2016. 35.9 fb^-1 of data was analyzed, and the search targeted pairs of jets and leptons, along with an invisible component. To account for experimental uncertainties, the data was adjusted to match expected standards in various scenarios. In a standard model interpretation, the results revealed that the cross-sectional values of Z + invisible and ZZ processes fell within expected ranges. Additionally, the results limited the cross-sectional values of simplified models of dark matter production, ranging from 10^-10 to 10^-6 pb, depending on the model. Finally, the results constrained the cross-sectional values of portal models, including a Higgs mediator, with excluded areas in mass-charge plane coverage. These findings contributed to our understanding of dark matter and the integrity of the standard model. Furthermore, the results established new benchmark marks for dark matter searches in similar processes at future colliders with higher energy levels. The analysis also validated the reliability of RecJet sub-categorization in dark matter searches and the stability of CMS jet reconstruction algorithms in this type of analysis. In a previous paper, Rawling and the current author established that a Banach space can be recovered from its compact stockings through a specific technique. Using ab initio calculations, we analyzed the epitaxial relationship and found that the van der Waals epitaxy is the most stable option. However, experimental samples exhibit a mixture of three epitaxy types, indicating a remote epitaxial relationship. To regulate the equilibrium, we analyzed the influence of a van der Waals gap on the epitaxial relationship and found that increasing the gap size favors remote epitaxy, while a gap size below 0.5 eA favors van der Waals epitaxy. This research provides a guideline for controlling the epitaxial relationship through substrate spacing. We analyze the behavior of the classical mean vector and covariance estimator in the context of multiple, heavily skewed time series data over a long period of time. As the observation period (n) increases, so does the number (d) of time sequences, leading to a non-stable matrix estimate. Typically, this matrix estimate is asymptotically equivalent to a multivariate matrix Gaussian distribution, but only if the (d) time sequences are independent of each other. Under the condition of weak dependence, the matrix estimate can be represented as a multivariate matrix with a long-tailed distribution. Specifically, for matrices with structure, such as variance or correlation, we show that the estimator's elements are independently and identically distributed with a long-tailed distribution, and that a long-tailed distribution principle applies to their second moments as well. As a result, the central limit theorem for the estimator's elements is not applicable, but we can demonstrate that a more complex distribution applies to their average squared values, which have a rate of convergence of n. This research was motivated by our analysis of the S&P 500 stock returns, as well as other economic time series, over a long period of time, which revealed significantly different results from those expected under a Gaussian distribution. In fact, our estimates for the mean vector and covariance matrix showed clear deviations from the expected behavior, prompting us to develop new theoretical methods and asymptotics. These results have implications for portfolio optimization, risk analysis, and other applications of multivariate time series analysis. Furthermore, our research is expected to contribute to the development of new statistical procedures and methods for heavily skewed, dependent time series data. As such, our research is expected to be of considerable interest to practitioners and theorists working with heavy-tailed financial and economic time series data. Internet Service Providers (ISPs) have long suffered from the phenomenon of congestion pricing, which clogs networks and results in poorer online experiences for end-users. A key innovation to address this issue involves Direct Data Exchange (DDE), a technology that enables content providers to establish private data channels with ISPs, allowing for optimized data transfer. This research delves into the challenges of revenue sharing between content and service providers in the presence of DDE. Specifically, we investigate whether content providers are willing to compensate ISPs for network access, given that DDE reduces congestion and improves the quality of online interactions. A critical aspect of our investigation is the impact of DDE on prices, as well as the position in which content providers negotiate revenue sharing agreements with ISPs. To address these inquiries, we develop a model that combines two distinct concepts: the Hotelling line model and the Shapley value model. Our analysis illustrates how the outcome changes when content providers no longer face congestion, as well as as when the network is congested. This analysis also demonstrates how the position of content providers in negotiations affects their willingness to compensate ISPs. Moreover, our findings highlight the difference in compensation payouts when content providers negotiate from the high or low end of the spectrum. Lastly, our investigation gauges the relative importance of individual content providers within the revenue sharing agreement payout. This research is the first of its kind to explore revenue sharing between content and service providers in the context of DDE. This paper presents an experimental evaluation of a trustworthiness metric proposed for second-price auctions. The evaluated metric aims to increase social welfare by prioritizing bidders who will remain in the auction. A novel auction format is introduced, where bidders are initially selected through a series of win-or-loss tournaments. Bidders who lose their initial tournament are given the option to re-enter the auction through an additional tournament. The selected bidders are then assigned prices determined by second-price auctions, with the option to withdraw from the auction without paying. A comprehensive laboratory experiment was conducted to evaluate the trustworthiness of this auction design. specific aspects of the auction design were altered in separate treatment sessions and bidders were offered incentives to record their true willingness-to-pay. The results demonstrate that the introduction of the withdrawal option does not affect bidders' willingness-to-pay, whereas the initial win-or-loss tournament induces bidders to prioritize short-term performance over long-term prospects. The proposed auction design outperforms the traditional second-price auction in terms of social welfare in scenarios where bidders prioritize short-term goals. However, the auction design falls short of the best possible performance when bidders are inherently motivated to maximize social welfare. The experiment's findings contribute to an understanding of the effects of incorporating time-sensitive elements and the possibility of leaving the auction when pricing mechanisms are used. Additionally, these results may be applied to design auctions that take into account bidders' long-term prospects in settings where such bidders can be identified. The proposed auction design is also relevant to environments where bidders can leave the auction and are rewarded based on their initial willingness-to-pay. Finally, these results may be applied to design auctions that take into account bidders' long-term prospects in settings where such bidders can be identified. The proposed auction design is also relevant to environments where bidders can leave the auction and are rewarded based on their initial willingness-to-pay. A key feature of this experiment is the varying number of bidders that are initially selected and added to the auction through win-or-loss tournaments. This is particularly useful from a theoretical standpoint as it enables a direct comparison with the results of continuous bidding mechanisms, where bidders can adjust their bids continuously rather than in win-or-loss tournaments. The experiment's design also incorporates bidders who are initially selected but do not enter the auction, as well as those who re-enter the auction through additional win-or-loss tournaments. This is particularly useful from a theoretical standpoint as it enables a direct comparison with the results of continuous bidding mechanisms, where bidders can adjust their bids

We explore an explanation for recent anomalies in $K$ and $B$ meson decays, assuming their non-SM scalar and vector particles have minimal parities. Their interactions, constrained by ground-state hadron masses, produce a unified set of $SU(2)_L$ representations for the scalar and vector fields, enabling a simultaneous fit to anomaly values in $K$ and $B$ systems. The results reveal the possibility of a $K$ anomaly solution with a minimal $K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0$ value and a $B$ anomaly solution with a moderately enhanced effective amplitude. The fit positions these new particles below the $W$ boson and identifies the lightest new particles as color-octet scalars with lifetimes amenable to study at future $e^+ e^-$ collider projects. Additionally, we examine in detail the predicted scalar and vector particle decays, particularly their rich dijet and tribaryon patterns, and propose a discovery strategy for these composite scalar and vector bosons at future $e^+ e^-$ collider projects with adequate beam polarization, utilizing dimuon and electron-positron final states to best identify these new parities. In conclusion, we find that the vectorlike composite model can concurrently explain the $K$ and $B$ anomalies, offering a promising framework for future searches at $e^+ e^-$ collider projects. The model also potentially addresses the 450 MeV dipion excess and offers new perspectives on hidden sectors. A follow-up study will investigate collider signals with adequate beam polarization to identify scalar and vector parities. The code for numerical fits is available at https://github.com/duodanwang/CompFit.git. A groundbreaking study was conducted to gather a vast collection of informative responses grounded in existing research, enabling them to be applied more broadly. Through the revision of 58 scientific papers, the research team compiled 1,594 queries and 7,894 responses, which were analyzed in detail. It was observed that the majority of these queries were speculative in nature, leading to three main areas of focus: (1) gathering basic information, (2) seeking examples, and (3) requesting clarification. To facilitate the utilization of these queries, they were categorized according to their content and paired with the relevant responses. These resources, along with the annotated data, are made accessible through http://infoseeking.dataforge.network and are designed to support human-like interactive tasks, including answering questions, summarizing content, and making summaries that can be supported by evidence. It is hoped that this collection will serve as a valuable benchmark for the development of AI systems, enabling them to engage in informative conversations that can be grounded in existing research. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widespread neurodevelopmental disorder commonly diagnosed in children, whose symptoms persist into adulthood. Conventional diagnostic methods for ADHD rely on clinical evaluation, including a detailed interview process called the Conners' Parent Questionnaire (CPQ). This study aims to improve ADHD diagnosis by integrating data-driven, neuroscience knowledge into a machine learning model. To achieve this, we employed a two-stage, enhanced classification system. Initially, rs-fMRI brain region selection was carried out using a forward feature selection method based on McNeill's et al. criteria. Subsequently, a 3D Convolutional Neural Network was trained on the resulting dataset to develop an rs-fMRI-derived algorithm for distinguishing ADHD and control groups. Notably, our approach demonstrated superior performance with an average accuracy of 87.84%, substantially outperforming the baseline model's accuracy without rs-fMRI data. Moreover, our comprehensive investigation into the chosen brain regions highlighted significant ADHD-related abnormalities in their connectivity. The selected ADHD-related regions included the left middle frontal gyrus, right middle frontal gyrus, and right inferior frontal gyrus, among others. These findings are presented and discussed in detail. Ultimately, this study showcases an innovative, enhanced machine learning method for diagnosing ADHD based on rs-fMRI data, which can facilitate more accurate condition identification while providing valuable insights into ADHD-related brain region interactions. It can be downloaded using the command 'git clone https://github.com/abdelrahmanomselmy/om_rsfMRI_ADHD.git'. This resource can support other researchers and developers in utilizing a similar approach to ours. They are characterized by integrated invariants of the bulk momentum-space Hamiltonian. A topological classification system predicts possible types of nodal surfaces, allowing for various applications in momentum-space topology. Recently, momentum-space nodal surfaces have been demonstrated and studied experimentally using photonic systems, crystal waveguides, and superconducting quantum circuits, opening doors for exploring momentum-space topology in systems that are easily manipulated and observed. This review covers the theoretical background, types of nodal surfaces, and provides an overview of the implemented experiments. It also discusses the potential for momentum-space topology in quantum circuits that incorporate interactive operations. This could enable the realization of momentum-space topological phenomena at an even higher level. Finally, the article concludes by highlighting the distinct features and potential applications of momentum-space nodal surfaces compared to conventional orbital nodal surfaces. They are particularly promising for applications such as momentum-space optical fibers, switches, and sensors. Additionally, they could enable novel phenomena like momentum-state entanglement and genuine momentum-space multiparton scattering. These potential applications are key to understanding the intrinsic properties of momentum-space nodal surfaces and the benefits they offer. the von Neumann entropy or logarithmic rank distribution within sublinear

entropy using $O(\sqrt{\log N}\cdot \log^3 N)$ queries, specifically for

for various important criteria. These results significantly outperform
existing classical methods, showcasing the greater expressiveness of
quantum algorithms in estimating crucial entropy properties. We demonstrate
the resilience of these schemes to noise resistant to quantum error correction.
We investigate the inherent limit of entropy estimation using $O(\log N)$
queries, validating the feasibility of our algorithmic approaches. The
research also develops the first quantum algorithms for estimating log-rank

Developing an efficient solver is crucial to take advantage of the processing power offered by these high-performance systems.  Although multilevel solvers are widely used in cardiac mechanics, research on them is limited. Our results indicate that our multilevel conditioner combines effectively with other multilevel solvers, but its combination with single-level methods reveals inherent limitations. The ever-growing amount of available data has made text-based information retrieval increasingly difficult, prompting the development of folksonomies - lightweight, user-generated systems that facilitate information access and sharing. Our study investigates key characteristics of folksonomies, aiming to identify best practices for designing and implementing effective folksonomies. Through data analysis and rankings, we evaluate and prioritize principles for designing successful folksonomies, including ensuring ease of use, maintaining system quality, enabling collaborative tagging, and providing functionality for discovering and connecting with other users. Our findings also highlight the importance of addressing issues related to usage, such as promoting the reuse of tags, promoting consistent timing of edits, and facilitating the exchange of interest among users. Furthermore, we identify opportunities for integrating existing knowledge management systems with folksonomies, and explore the potential for employing folksonomies as a means of promoting user engagement and participation in data management systems. Our study is the first to apply the methods of the evaluation and design of interactive systems to the domain of folksonomies. Through an empirical analysis of our data sets and results, we establish a set of design principles for guiding the creation and implementation of effective folksonomies. Our contribution to this research involves identifying key challenges related to the evolution of folksonomies, and proposing a theoretical framework for explaining the behavior and development of these systems. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, which can incorporate knowledge from previous experiences to perform well on novel tasks. To address this issue, a realistic evaluation framework, called L2Explorer, is presented, which supports the testing of these lifelong reinforcement learning methods. By utilizing a diverse range of skills, L2Explorer simulates scenarios that mimic real-world scenarios, including multi-task scenarios and sequential learning. Additionally, it enables the evaluation of models across a range of metrics, including their generalization abilities, their ability to perform well in the absence of experience, and their performance when faced with an endless stream of tasks. To further enhance research in this area, a comprehensive suite of benchmark problems, known as the Continuous General Assessment of Reinforcement Learning, or CGARL, is also introduced. This set of problems, which can be accessed through a public interface, tests a model's performance across a range of challenging tasks, including those requiring exploration, high-dimensional state spaces, and rapidly changing dynamics. Research using L2Explorer and CGARL has shown that existing models fall short when faced with these types of problems. This work now offers an open-source tool, based on PyTorch, for studying these challenging problems and evaluating the latest models. A range of experimental studies have been conducted using this framework to assess various models and evaluate their continuous learning capabilities. Notably, a model built using a combination of experience replay, neural network-based models, and the A2C algorithm has outperformed other leading models when tested on these problems. A combination of the runtime evaluations from these studies, along with an initial assessment of their source code, has led to a preliminary ranking of the relative effectiveness of 54 evaluated models. This work now offers an open-source tool, based on PyTorch, for training and evaluating these models in a unified manner. A model based on the PPO-Hybrid algorithm, which combines experience replay, neural network-based models, and several other key components, has emerged as a top-performing model in initial evaluations. Future work using this framework will focus on assessing other leading models and evaluating their continuous learning capabilities. This research focuses on finding the boundary between two differently composed media, 
with known material properties, by using transmission eigenfunctions.
These functions satisfy both an elliptic equation and a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map,
which is determined by the boundary conditions.
As a result, identifying the boundary becomes a spectral problem,
involving the transmission eigenvalues.
To approach this problem, 
we use an asymptotic analysis to find an approximate boundary,
and then develop a graphical method to improve this approximation.
 ultimately proving that the exact boundary can be uniquely determined. 
To demonstrate the method's effectiveness,
we provide examples of transmission eigenfunctions in spherically stratified media.

We introduce the active graph message transfer network (AGMTN), an adaptive graph message passing neural network designed for visual recognition tasks. The AGMTN consists of an initial graph message passing module, followed by repeated iterations of alternating graph message passing and aggregation modules. Each graph message passing module can be customized to suit specific tasks.
