Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity to their vertices.

A previously developed approach by Bishop and Sardinha for average-case problems revealed that, in certain situations, PTAS can be derived without explicitly determining the optimal solution density, as this parameter can be estimated based on the problem's formulation.

This research develops a precise framework to derive PTAS for average-case problems involving specific objective functions and graph classes characterized by vertex-independent structure, allowing for the utilization of local sparsity measures, such as the vertex degree, to approximate solution density.

As a proof-of-concept, the authors successfully obtain a PTAS for the Minimum Vertex Spanner Approximation problem in sparse graphs, achieving a gap of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ for approximate solutions, where the gap is defined as the ratio of approximate to exact cost. This result is also extended to weighted CSPs, yielding a PTAS with a gap of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{m})$ for such problems, where $m$ represents the number of edges in the graph. The findings provide positive results for problems that are likely NP-hard in the sparse regime, such as Minimum Vertex Spanner Approximation, and extend negative results for dense instances of these problems, as proven in prior works. The PTAS derived in this research also imply the existence of efficient algorithms for estimating solution density and applying it towards a FPTAS, which was not previously known. The approach developed can potentially be generalized to derive PTAS for other graph classes, subject to specific density measures. The authors also investigate the feasibility of deriving PTAS for dense instances of problems, but unfortunately could not obtain it in this case. The paper leaves open the question of whether PTAS can be obtained for a broader class of problems with at least polynomially bounded solution density. To facilitate effective session-based suggestion, users need relevant information at the session level, and recommendations should be tailored to each user's unique preferences by taking into account their current session contents. Prior studies on session-based suggestion have employed various strategies, but these approaches still fall short in addressing two critical challenges: 1) obtaining sufficient labeled data, and 2) presenting accurate suggestions in real-time. To address the first challenge, this research presents a new dataset, and to tackle the second challenge, this paper proposes an innovative method called Self-Guided Graph Co-Training (SGCT), which enables session-based suggestion through an unsupervised learning approach. SGTC leverages two interconnected networks - a session-guided graph to capture dynamic session patterns and a user-guided graph to extract user preferences. By combining the two networks, this method can provide relevant suggestions. To ensure seamless user interactions, this method also employs real-time recommendation techniques. Experimental results confirm that SGTC surpasses existing methods in both accuracy and speed. Notably, this method can present recommendations within 1ms, and these recommendations receive 25% higher engagement rates compared to other approaches. Evaluation metrics also indicate that SGTC achieves 0.134 and 0.118 higher accuracy than other methods at the session and user levels, respectively. To validate the efficacy of SGTC, this research conducts both controlled experiments and a field study. Results from the field study demonstrate that users prefer SGTC over other methods, and when SGTC is employed, users demonstrate 120% higher conversion rates and 48% increased engagement rates. Furthermore, this method also boosts overall interaction quality by 30%. Additionally, this research validates the authenticity of the newly created dataset using three validation techniques. Validation results confirm that the new dataset is authentic and exhibits characteristics distinct from existing datasets. To showcase the practical applications and usability of SGTC, this research presents a series of interactive figures and case studies highlighting the method's ability to present relevant suggestions for various user actions and how these suggestions facilitate seamless interaction. Additionally, this research demonstrates that SGTC can automatically detect when to provide user-driven suggestions and when to employ session-based suggestions. To enable smooth user experiences, this method also employs an innovative memory mechanism that assists in data encoding and retrieval. Notably, SGTC can persistently provide relevant suggestions even when users encounter network disruptions. This phenomenon is attributed to the emergence of localized modes at two points when correlations become dominant, resulting in two isolated regions separated by a central point. We established a condition for minimizing the eigenvalue exception at zero energy and found this condition to be analogous to the one found in free systems without non-Hermitian effects. We further demonstrated that correlations can reduce the overall scaling exponent of the system's localized states. Most importantly, our study reveals that correlations can eliminate the skin effect in the absence of chiral symmetry, and conversely, result in a skin effect at low system sizes when chiral symmetry is present. These outcomes have important implications for understanding the topological characteristics of correlated systems and their potential applications in experiments. Additionally, this study provides a basis for investigating correlations in higher-dimensional systems with various types of symmetry. Changes in hyperspectral images over time can be utilized in various applications such as tracking alterations in environments, assessing damages after disasters, and monitoring urban developments. However, automating the process of alteration detection in hyperspectral images remains a complex task due to the need to effectively combine temporal image pairs, accommodate diverse alteration types, and pinpoint precise alteration locations. Current methods employing deep learning techniques, such as Convolutional Autoencoders (CAEs), have limitations in alteration detection as they fail to account for the spatial relationships within pixels and the distinct spectral and spatial characteristics of alteration areas. To address these limitations, we introduce an unsupervised alteration detection method using Feature Combination deep Convolutional Autoencoders (FCCA) that combines spectral and spatial information and select optimal pixels to guide the alteration area extraction. Our method achieves improved performance compared to other tested techniques on various urban and natural alteration scenarios. For example, when evaluating a image of Berlin's famous Brandenburger Tor, our FCCA successfully locate the exact alteration areas. Our method also outperforms other tested techniques by achieving accurate results even when subjected to noise and diverse alteration scenarios. Our source code is publicly available for other researchers to reproduce our results. Our experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a consistent and high accuracy of 98.5% or higher for a wide range of tested images. Additionally, our results also include the reconstruction of original and altered images as well as the extraction of relevant pixel features. Our findings further analyze and evaluate the distinct spectral and spatial characteristics of various alteration areas using the learned pixel weights. Our investigation into the generalization of our method reveals that our FCCA can effectively detect alterations in diverse images of Berlin, captured under different conditions. Our method can be adapted for real-world applications, such as Land Use Change detection, where it can learn to recognize distinct categories of alterations. Our findings also open up new directions for research, such as incorporating prior knowledge into the deep CAE model for further improvement in performance. Our overall goal is to develop a robust, unsupervised, and efficient method for hyperspectral alteration detection that can be employed in a wide range of real-world scenarios. A particular type of smooth projective variety, which holds significant importance in algebraic geometry, is examined in this paper. This examination reveals that such varieties with numerous points in a finite field, as well as positive-dimensional varieties, possess a distinct characteristic – they are incapable of hosting an embedding into another, smaller, variety, as specified by a particular condition. This finding yields significant consequences in various disciplines, including number theory, where it sheds light on a long-standing, previously unresolved issue concerning the transference degree of certain polynomial systems. This, in turn, facilitates the resolution of several related questions and provides an accurate calculation of the transference degree for specific, two-variable algebraic varieties, which serves as a key contribution of this paper. Finally, several diagnostic tests to determine whether a variety satisfies the required condition have been devised, utilizing concepts from intersection theory and rational points. This study further clarifies the relationship between the condition and another, previously established criterion – the vanishing of certain cohomology groups – providing essential insights and examples that bridge the gap between these two theories. This work presents a comprehensive review of the existing literature on the condition and its various equivalences, as well as the significance of this research. Specifically, it encompasses the works of Boguski, Eisenbud, Green, Hartshorne, Hatcher, Lerman, Miranda, Rothstein, Serre, Ulmer, Vakil, and Zamboni. This enigmatic entity has long been a source of confusion, particularly as classical objects are described in terms of quantum fields, implying that the spacetime itself is imbued with quantum properties. We have translated the Scott framework for PCF into univalent type theory, and we have done so in a way that is fully formalized using the Coq proof assistant.  This translation preserves the original operational and denotational semantics, and it leverages univalence by employing a type of types that is closed under the formation of product, sum, and dependent sum types.  Moreover, we have derived from the translation a type-theoretic version of the Curry-Howard correspondence, which reflects the relationship between PCF's base and recursive types with their corresponding elements.  Our work has also shown that a type of types can be used to model a non-uniquely determined type, and it has provided a type-theoretic explanation for the $T$-$\aleph_0$ combinator.  Furthermore, we have carried out a forking lifting lemma, which allows a type of types to be extended with new types constructed through application, and we have used this extension to model a form of call-by-need semantics.  This extension has also enabled the identification of a type-theoretic version of the $S$-$\aleph_0$ combinator.  Through our work, we hope to contribute to the development of a type-theoretic foundation for programming languages with higher-order and recursive features, and we hope to provide a type-theoretic framework for modeling various forms of computation within univalence.  This framework can potentially be generalized to model other programming languages within univalence, and it can serve as a foundation for a type-theoretic specification of programming languages that is based on univalence.  Moreover, the types and proof that we have used can potentially be applied to other domains that involve modeling data types through types.  This includes modeling data for various types of speculative science, as well as modeling various types of computation in physics and other fields.  This means that the techniques that we have used and the insights that we have gained can potentially be applied to other areas beyond programming languages and recursion. The direct photon coalignment in copper-copper collisions at a center of mass energy of 200 GeV was measured by the PHENIX experiment at a collision energy of 200 GeV. In copper-copper collisions, photons serve as ideal indicators of the collision fireball, whereas electrons and muons originate from both primary interactions and photon decays. By analyzing charged particle spectra in the range of 1 to 5 GeV/c, and employing a relativistic transport model, the primary photon production rate was determined. By subtracting the photon contributions from electron and muon spectra, the direct photon coalignment was calculated. It shows alignment within the experimental uncertainties, ranging from 100 millionths to 3 thousandths, depending on the collision energy and rapidity. This measurement is compared to a relativistic transport model and to previous measurements in gold-gold and proton-proton collisions. It suggests that a relativistic transport model can effectively explain direct photon coalignment in copper-copper collisions at a collision energy of 200 GeV. Furthermore, photon coalignment exhibits an inverse relationship with collision energy and rapidity. The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to find the highest ratio of the volume to the edge count among simple polyhedra, featuring all distinct edge lengths, and at least one edge shared between any two given vertices. In their seminal work from 1948, Turan proposed this problem, and it remains unresolved to this day. Our research provides a solution, demonstrating that any such polyhedron with large volume and small $\epsilon$ must have edge count close to $O(N^2)$, where $N$ represents the number of vertices. The proof relies on an interesting application of the $\ell_2$-norm to design an efficient sampling strategy. The obtained estimate was previously shown to be exact, with $N^2$ being the lowest possible edge count for large $N$, thanks to constructions by Gromov, Alon-Shelah, and Allen-Kinnebrew. Our work generalizes the $\ell_2$-norm approach, originally used in a different problem by the first author and Matulis, to the field of combinatorial geometry, yielding an independent and surprisingly simple result. Theoretical predictions about pulsar wind nebulae, specifically their gamma-ray emission, have driven research in this field for over a decade. Models based on primary and secondary radiation can explain observed characteristics, but predicting precise pulsar wind nebula shapes and patterns remains challenging. Despite these difficulties, astronomers can use detailed computer simulations to model specific sources, such as the TeV blob associated with the pulsar PSR J1589+5629, and learn more about its potential origin. Could this'mysterious' structure actually be a pulsar wind nebula from a companion pulsar, or perhaps a supernova remnant interacting with these cosmic objects? To resolve this mystery, astronomers can analyze the characteristics of the structure and its associated pulsar, as well as nearby supernova remnants, using detailed computer models and observational data. Ultimately, the most plausible explanation for the TeV blob is that it is a bridge of gamma-ray emission between two pulsar wind nebulae, and specifically the wind nebula of PSR J1589+5629 and PSR J1620-5206, at their point of interaction in the larger supernova remnant G359.63-0.03. This theory is supported by the structure's alignment with the western edge of the supernova remnant and its proximity to the predicted wind nebula of PSR J1620-5206, as well as its gamma-ray emission pattern, which would result from the overlap of the two wind nebulae. This explanation is further supported by the structure's appearance as a single, elongated region of gamma-ray emission, and the potential presence of a second, smaller wind nebula within the TeV blob area. This could be the wind nebula of an as-yet-uncalled pulsar, likely a slow pulsar with a spin-down age of approximately 50 ky and a magnetic field of approximately 2 x 10^13 Gauss. To confirm this theory, astronomers can use the search for pulsar wind nebulae and the predicted location of the missing pulsar wind nebula within the supernova remnant G359.63-0.03. This would be the second time a missing pulsar wind nebula has been predicted using the gamma-ray emission of a TeV blob, following the wind nebula of PSR J1846+5752 in the supernova remnant G182.0+5.0. This potential second discovery would further solidify the link between supernova remnants and gamma-ray pulsar wind

In 2007, a giant radio galaxy with a 6.7 million parsec span was discovered 
in the prototype of the Faint Radio Sky Survey, J2102+6015, at a z = 4.575. 
Initially classified as an active galactic nucleus (AGN), it possessed 
characteristic broad-band spectrum distinct from lower redshift objects. 
Further analysis involved re-examining the data from multiple radio surveys, 
including FIRST and NVSS, at a higher resolution than before. This was 
accompanied by precise positions and flux densities for J2102+6015 and 
its sub-components. Additionally, a detailed search through optical and X-ray 
catalogs yielded no significant results. Further examination using custom 
software revealed the galaxy has two distinct sub-components. 
J2102+6015's sub-system exhibits diffuse emission along a 1.7 million parsec 
tract, and is thought to be the result of a youthful diffuse emission system 
shared with another component. Both systems are thought to be the result of 
recollimation by interactions with the intergalactic medium. 
Conversely, the galaxy's central component displays symmetrical, jet-like 
emission, shared with another object at a lower redshift. This classification 
of J2102+6015 as a diffuse galaxy is a "judgement reversal" compared to 
initially classified as an AGN. 
Lastly, J2102+6015's 20 cm faintest component, located at the galaxy's core, 
displayed an extraordinary amount of spectral index variation over its 
extended emission. This could be attributed to its core emission being 
overpowered by diffuse emission. 
J2102+6015's 4.575 z holds the record for the highest redshift of a giant 
radio galaxy that isn't part of a cluster. Its distinct, high-redshift 
phenomenon is likely to be part of a lesser-known, "youthful" giant radio 
galaxy class. This phenomenon is thought to be the result of brief, high-speed 
particle acceleration in galaxies. Upon entering the neutral intergalactic 
medium, these particles collide and release energy into the surroundings, 
creating diffuse emission. This process is temporary, and J2102+6015's 
classification as an AGN was a "youthful" illusion.

Patients with non-small cell lung cancer are often predicted to be lung cancer free if they meet certain criteria determined by the American Society of Clinical Oncology. The accuracy of this prediction depends on specific characteristics of small cell non-small cell lung cancers, such as the size and location of the tumor lymph nodes. Current methods rely solely on numerical data from computed tomography scans, neglecting the visual aspects of the scans. Our research involves developing artificial intelligence models that consider both numerical and visual elements from CT scans to improve the accuracy of prognosing how effective a certain treatment will be for patients with non-small cell lung cancer.
The proposed approach analyzes both numerical and visual elements from CT scans to predict the likelihood of patients with NSCLC being lung cancer free with a specific treatment. The model uses multiple modalities, including various numerical characteristics and the images within the CT scans themselves, to make more informed predictions. Our teams created four different models, leveraging numerical data, image data, combined modalities, and attention-based multi-modalities to make predictions. To compare the effectiveness of these models, we conducted experiments using data from patients with NSCLC, evaluating the models based on their ability to predict cancer-free outcomes and their performance with and without attention mechanisms. The models were evaluated based on their precision, recall, F1 score, ACC, and Brier score across different thresholds related to cancer-free outcomes. Our multi-modal approach demonstrated better performance compared to models relying solely on numerical or image data, resulting in improved precision, recall, F1 score, ACC, and Brier score. Additionally, the addition of an attention mechanism further enhanced the model's performance in noisy cases, leading to increased precision, recall, F1 score, ACC, and Brier score. Therefore, multi-modal deep learning architectures that consider both numerical and visual elements from CT scans offer more accurate predictions of lung cancer free outcomes for patients with a specific type of non-small cell lung cancer. Natural language understanding is a fundamental element of numerous natural language processing applications and plays a significant role in various tasks that involve language.
Despite its importance, it is often overlooked in studies related to natural language processing and reinforcement learning.
This paper provides a comprehensive summary of the authentic methods for representing and modeling language, highlighting their advantages and limitations, in order to encourage the development of effective techniques for natural language processing tasks that involve reinforcement learning. Additionally, we present challenges associated with natural language and potential areas for improvement in the representation and modeling of language to support more robust reinforcement learning techniques. Furthermore, we outline promising avenues for further research in this area, backed by relevant examples, in order to stimulate advancement in the field. A publicly accessible repository containing detailed references to the discussed topics has been made available. 

\textbf{Keywords:} Language modeling, Reinforcement learning, Natural language understanding, Authentic approaches, State representation, Natural language processing.

A reliable and efficient data exchange is crucial for various emerging technologies like semantic orthogonal frequency division multiplexing, which requires data to be transmitted based on pre-agreed meaning between the transmitter and receiver. However, conventional semantic communication systems rely on uncertain channel conditions that can lead to incorrect data interpretation by the receiver, resulting in significant data loss and reduced performance. Furthermore, current research often relies on costly cognitive abilities, which is impractical for wide-scale implementation. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that combines neuro-symbolic communication to enable reliable data exchange without requiring prior agreements. We develop a neuro-symbolic learning framework, which allows the transmitter and receiver to independently discover a shared understanding through mutual interaction. Our approach achieves this goal by modeling the data exchange as a signaling game, which is solved using a neuro-symbolic policy gradient method. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms conventional semantic communication systems, delivering higher data transfer rates and lower error rates without needing prior agreements. Additionally, we show that the emergent signaling schemes learned by the transmitters and receivers converge rapidly to a shared understanding. These findings provide new avenues for data exchange in dynamic environments and enable reliable communication among devices with limited prior knowledge. Recent advancements in session-based suggestion systems have led to the development of a two-phase strategy for personalized recommendation, initially employing session prediction models to generate candidate sessions and then ranking them using user-specific models. However, the initial strategy's reliance on session-based models has several drawbacks, primarily its inability to effectively tailor suggestions to users' long-term preferences. In an effort to address these issues, researchers have introduced three novel session-based suggestion methods that produce candidate sessions as input for the two-phase suggestion framework. These new methods utilize session encoders to generate sessions and incorporate user and item features, thereby enabling more accurate ranking and an improvement in suggestion accuracy. Furthermore, the researchers introduced three additional ranking models to augment the two-phase suggestion framework's candidate ranking phase. Our proposed method earned top rankings in an online evaluation of recommender systems, surpassing established benchmarks. In particular, our method exhibited superior performance compared to two established session-based suggestion methods, ultimately resulting in a 25% improvement in accuracy over the simplest of these methods. In the second experiment, our additional ranking models significantly enhanced suggestion accuracy when evaluated against a baseline that utilized only the original ranking model. This research introduces an innovative framework for coordinating a swarm of autonomous drones, ensuring they navigate through pre-defined cell structures without colliding with each other. An algorithm has been developed to tackle this problem, ensuring the accuracy of the cellular structure model and ensuring safe drone interactions. These goals are achieved by converting the registration problem into a point-to-point correspondence challenge, using centroid-based methods to guide the registration process. To validate the framework's effectiveness, simulations are employed to test its robustness under varying noise levels. Moreover, experiments are conducted using real drones to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method in practical applications. Comprehensive evaluation tests are performed to showcase the algorithm's robustness in dealing with diverse scenarios, including the movement of drones within the cells. Results indicate that the proposed method exhibits nearly perfect registration accuracy, with an optimal mean squared error of 0.057, achieved using 10 iterations of the algorithm. Consequently, it enables a swarm of drones to accurately follow the predefined cellular structure, ensuring safe and collaborative flight. These experiments also identify the optimal algorithm parameters, including a 0.001 Gaussian noise standard deviation, used throughout the testing process. With an average processing time of 103.81 ms, the proposed method showcases the feasibility of real-time application using modern computing devices. Overall, this research presents a novel coordination algorithm for swarms of drones, ensuring they maintain a cellular structure, avoid collisions, and demonstrate robust performance in the presence of noise. Additionally, it facilitates general movement within the cells using the registered point cloud, demonstrated through practical drone tests. In machine learning, knowledge transfer allows models to exploit information from other models, often achieving better results.  Most knowledge transfer studies have concentrated on using data to move information between models.  In contrast, this research explores the possibility of transferring knowledge without data, relying solely on evaluation outcomes.  Using a black-box framework that makes decisions based on input, we developed a zero-shot knowledge transfer technique that extracts relevant information from successful models and applies it to new situations without prior experience.  The technique does not require detailed insight into either the successful models or the new situations.  Testing the approach using decision-making sets, we found that it consistently performs as well or better than models trained using the new data from scratch.  Additionally, we found that it also offers significant benefits over methods that move information using data.  To validate the findings, we tested the approach using a range of scenarios, including cases where the new situations have similar characteristics to the data used to train the successful models and cases where the new situations are very different.  The study shows that under both circumstances, the technique achieves better results than models trained using the new data from scratch.  The work described represents the first successful use of a decision-based black-box framework for transferring information without data, relying solely on evaluation outcomes.  The technique does not require detailed insight into either the successful models or the new situations and consistently performs as well or better than models trained using the new data from scratch.  The results validate the relevance of the decision-based black-box framework for a variety of applications. A geometric interpretation of geometric T-duality for tori with flat connections is established, generalizing the classical geometric formulation.  This interpretation applies to a broad class of twisted tori, encompassing both the simple and double coverings of non-Abelian groups.  To achieve this, a suitable generalization of the torus geometry is developed, compatible with the singular hermitian structure required for geometric symmetry breaking.  This includes a twisted version of the flat connection equation, resulting in the BPS equation in four dimensions, and a corresponding moduli space description.  This geometric interpretation of geometric T-duality is found to coincide with the gauge theory formulation in the literature, and shares many properties with the flat connection moduli space.  Specifically, the twisted torus moduli space inherits key properties from the flat connection moduli space, and exhibits a mixture of finite and infinite discrete symmetries, partly geometric and non-geometric, depending on the bundle structure.  In the case of the chiral clock chain, this geometric interpretation yields a hidden $\mathbb{Z}_{N_c}$ symmetry, previously uncovered through matrix product state analysis.  Furthermore, the twisted torus moduli space is shown to accommodate a generalized concept of elliptic curves, extending established principles to the non-Abelian case.  This geometric interpretation of geometric T-duality also enables a simplified understanding of duality chains and exceptional Janus cases, as demonstrated for various examples in one, two, and three dimensions.  Finally, the applied methods and mathematical frameworks are outlined, demonstrating how geometric symmetry breaking and geometric T-duality can be described using generalized geometric structures, and providing a uniform approach to addressing questions of duality and breaking.

This paper proposes an innovative metric for assessing code performance that seamlessly integrates parity-check code analysis with channel modeling, thereby streamlining decoding evaluations. Unlike traditional bit-error rates, our metric facilitates straightforward comparisons between different codes and decoding methods. Unlike more advanced metrics like union bounds, our approach doesn't require intricate interleaving analysis, yet still accurately models code performance and decoder restrictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our metric through numerical examples, where it successfully predicts PAC code performance and identifies optimal decoding strategies. Furthermore, our metric enables the calculation of minimum distances and error probabilities for PAC codes with varying densities, including those that don't support density evolution methods. We illustrate the utility of our metric in estimating PAC code performance under unknown channel conditions, thereby demonstrating its potential as a real-time PAC code decoder metric. We also explore the intersection of our metric's techniques with existing PAC code analysis methods that utilize density evolution and/or check-node messages, revealing new perspectives and avenues for integration. Finally, we examine the metric's applicability to codes beyond parity-check codes, revealing its general applicability to any code that can be efficiently checked for errors. This encompasses popular code types like LDPC, LCD, LRCH, LRI, LDGM, and regular PC codes. The proposed metric is made freely available through our website. We also make publicly available our previously published research on PAC Codes, which includes performance predictions, new architectures, and novel decoding methods. We hope this publicly available repository will aid researchers and engineers in quickly accessing our prior work and viewing it in context with the new approaches we are introducing. We anticipate our metric will become a standard tool in contemporary parity-check code research and development, thereby expanding its existing impact. Additionally, we envision it will inspire new directions of inquiry, thereby expanding the paradigm of parity-check code analysis and design. We expect this expanded paradigm to encompass not just code performance, but also novel architectures and decoding methods that were previously difficult to evaluate. We illustrate this through several examples, including density-evolution-based codes that were previously difficult to analyze using traditional metrics. The developed algorithm navigates the limitations of wearable PCG technology by forming a model of the hand and its interactions with objects within a sequence of point clouds. The algorithm's primary objectives are to accurately identify and synchronize the hand and object geometry in each frame, and to reconstruct their original shapes at the starting frame. The method relies on a unified surface model that incorporates the wearer's hand and any visible objects, and involves removing the wearer's hand from the point clouds to create a sparse surface model. The wearing hand's surface model is generated using a PCG-friendly template and optimized through registration with the dense surface model. The algorithm demonstrated exceptional performance on a unique dataset consisting of hundreds of sequences, each with thousands of frames, showcasing diverse objects and hand poses through wearable PCG technology. The method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, averaging only 0.75 cm reconstruction error for the wearing hand's surface model, and 1.13 cm for non-wearing objects. By using a depth camera to capture robot-independent images, the experiment demonstrates that the estimated coordinates can be accurately calculated and aligned uniformly, even in scenarios with multiple tables and varied object patterns. A model that assumes neighboring treatment assignments to given units can help identify potential interference effects has been proposed, but it lacks a clear way to test this assumption. We provide conditions under which this model's assumptions can be verified by comparing treated and control groups without involving the units that directly received treatment. We also discuss the practical challenges of implementing these conditions, especially when working with uncontrolled data, and demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through simulations using a high-dimensional dataset. Finally, we apply this model to real-world data from a school-based vaccination study, revealing significant evidence of interference effects and the importance of considering such effects when evaluating educational policies. In particular, we found that when focusing on a specific outcome of interest, high doses of the vaccine led to significant declines in related outcomes among non-vaccinated students, but this effect was not seen in a second, unrelated outcome. Our work offers a first approach to testing the assumptions of this model and provides further insight into the causes of non-ignorability in a high-dimensional setting. Additionally, this study contributes to the understanding of potential interference effects in educational settings, shedding light on the potential benefits and harms of widespread adoption of vaccines in this domain. The associated package RSCI contains the necessary code to implement these methods and examples under regular conditions, as well as the data used in our study, which can be found at https://github.com/awalton6/Nearest-Neighbors-Treatment-Interference/tree/main/packages/RSCI. This data also includes additional results not mentioned in the paper, such as further analysis of our model's performance when applied to a second vaccine dose. Furthermore, the package includes a detailed mathematical review of the model and its associated conditions, which can be referred to for further clarification on our results. Finally, the package includes example code for reproducing our figures and running additional simulations using our model. The model's assumption that nearby treatment assignments can help identify potential interference effects has been widely adopted in various applications, but its theoretical underpinnings have only been explored in limited contexts, specifically those involving a small number of treated units and a large number of control groups. We provide a more general approach to the model's assumption, valid under a wide range of treatment assignments and outcome responses, and demonstrate the efficacy of this model through simulations using a high-dimensional dataset. Calculations of neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilating within a Neutron Star offer a viable method for detecting DM via a Neutron Star's variable brightness. This involves DM interacting with nucleons via a mediator particle, and while a gauge boson mediator mediates the most visible neutrino emissions, a pseudoscalar mediator can produce non-relativistic corrections, making this interaction potentially more significant at lower temperatures. Researchers have demonstrated that in a gauge boson-mediated DM model, its strength is limited by neutron star stability, but in a pseudoscalar model, this constraint doesn't apply, allowing for a larger parameter space and more considerable neutrino emissions. Moreover, within a pseudoscalar model, its strength can be tied to the DM's mass splitting, and this can lead to a considerable enhancement of neutrino emissions compared to a gauge boson model. This leads to a potential for up to $10^{51}$ neutrino ergs per second in a pseudoscalar model, which is notably higher than the $10^{49}$ neutrino ergs per second produced in a gauge boson model. This increased emissions in a pseudoscalar model could make a gauge boson model more easily detectable. To differentiate between these two models, detecting the signature of multiple neutrino flavors could help identify a pseudoscalar model, whereas a gauge boson model would only produce a single neutrino type. Additionally, by comparing the DM's direct detection cross-section in a pseudoscalar model to a gauge boson model, this enhanced neutrino emissions in a pseudoscalar model leads to a $10^7$ to $10^10$ fold increase in the required direct detection cross-section to reach the same neutrino emission threshold. This means a future direct detection experiment could potentially rule out a pseudoscalar model based on its neutrino emissions. In applications requiring genuine randomness, the conventional approach typically involves external memory or specialized hardware at a considerable cost in terms of space, speed, and complexity. This limitation becomes particularly significant when compact system size is a priority, such as in bio-electronic implants where memory-based true random numbers are in high demand to secure medical treatments. This challenge can be addressed through a novel method called TuRaN, which leverages a unique undervoltage scaling technique to harness SRAM's inherent randomness. TuRaN utilizes a temperature-dependent threshold voltage that activates a binary stochastic process within the SRAM cells. By implementing a selective read-out mechanism for random bits, TuRaN achieves an operational speed of 1 MS/s while maintaining an error rate below 10^-3. Furthermore, TuRaN's read-out energy consumption is remarkably low, at approximately 30 pJ/bit, and the process occurs within the existing SRAM cells that underpin modern VLSI designs. As such, TuRaN offers a highly secure and efficient method for genuine randomness generation, tailored to meet the specialized needs of nano-electronics in the realm of bio-medical applications. However, this approach may also find suitable applications in a broad range of domains, such as cryptography, provable security, and randomized protocols. Experimental results validate TuRaN's feasibility and demonstrate its potential as a standard feature in SRAM cells to facilitate secure and efficient randomness generation. TuRaN's integration can significantly boost the security of compact electronic systems, such as bio-electronic implants, while also reducing their bandwidth consumption due to the reduced data transfer rate required. As such, TuRaN stands out as a novel method for harnessing SRAM's inherent randomness to meet the specialized needs of secure and efficient nano-electronics. Still, its applications extend beyond the realm of bio-medical applications, also encompassing domains like cryptography, randomized protocols, and provable security. TuRaN's read-out mechanism, including its theoretical foundations and experimental results, is discussed in detail in this research paper, which highlights the approach's potential for securely enabling randomness in compact electronic systems without energy-consuming external components. In various studies, the tendency of complex neural networks to discover straightforward solutions has been observed, yet the underlying reason for this phenomenon remains poorly understood. We found that this behavior can be explained by the discovery of multiple interpretable representations within the neural network. These representations simplify the task at hand, often by reducing the input data dimensionality or identifying irrelevant information. We demonstrated this effect in three different scenarios - discovering a normal distribution in latent variables, selecting only necessary inputs, and discovering structured data relationships - and showcased its significance through the improvement of concept alignment, where one's latent variables are connected to another's. We also developed an algorithm based on this finding, allowing neural networks to discover these beneficial representations automatically. This work provides a foundation for future research on the regularization effects of neural networks' internal representations. The code for our experiments is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jjgordon/latent-regex. The data used in our research can be found at https://doi.org/10.6084/m1.fw6084. We also offer a demonstration of our findings on TensorFlow Hub at https://tfhub.dev/jjgordon/neural-regex/1. The mathematical principles underlying our research are described in Appendix 1, while additional explanations and visualizations are presented in Appendices 2-6. Lastly, the text of this paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01333. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of generative models, such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and Normalizing Flows, which can be used for unsupervised learning of high-dimensional and complex datasets. However, prior work primarily employed these models within standalone frameworks, neglecting their potential for collaborative learning with established supervised models. This study demonstrates that, in fact, VAEs and variational flows can be integrated into various supervised learning frameworks, notably improving upon existing models when data is annotated insufficiently. Our work also introduces an innovative hybrid model, "Hydra," which fuses a neural network with a normalizing flow, enabling the efficient learning of complex datasets through an iterative process involving multiple passes through the data. When applied to 2D image synthesis, Hydra outperforms HyDrAx, a variation of Hydra that incorporates adversarial training, and competes favorably with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) on labeled data. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub. Our findings show that HyDrAx and Hydra can generate synthetic images by iterating through a dataset of size 104, delivering image quality on par with state-of-the-art GANs, even when trained on labeled data. In addition, a comprehensive evaluation of 3D image synthesis on MRI datasets revealed that Hydra can be an effective method for performing unsupervised and semi-supervised learning, often outperforming HyDrAx and VAEs. Moreover, a semi-supervised learning assessment using Incidental Pregnancy dataset demonstrated that Hydra can be an efficient and reliable method, consistently achieving results comparable to or better than HyDrAx and VAEs. It is worth noting that, in the case of labeled data, HyDrAx can sometimes perform worse than VAEs or GANs due to overfitting. Nonetheless, this issue can be mitigated through an analysis of the dataset and the removal of redundant information, thereby enabling the unsupervised learning of a reduced set of latent variables. Our work indicates that normalizing flows can be integrated into various learning frameworks to facilitate collaborative learning and, in certain scenarios, enable the efficient unsupervised learning of high-dimensional and complex datasets. Moreover, a hybrid model (Hydra) can be employed for synthetic data generation, offering advantages such as reduced memory requirements and faster data access. Recent research has highlighted the effectiveness of in-context learning, a method utilizing few-shot experiments with pre-trained language models to generate responses. A key aspect of in-context learning has gone largely unstudied: the influence of training corpora on the performance of these models. In this study, we investigate whether altering a model's training dataset affects its capabilities in-context. Our findings indicate that adjusting the training dataset's characteristics and incorporating diverse knowledge into the model can significantly boost its performance. Notably, incorporating a wide range of knowledge, such as detailed encyclopedic entries, enables the model to access information not present in the in-context prompts. In contrast, a dataset focused solely on one-word meanings falls short of the model's full potential. Based on these observations, we suggest that in-context learning can be viewed as a form of query-specific retrieval, where the model's success relies on its ability to recognize relevant information within its training data. Our study also discovers that a model pre-trained on diverse data, including images and music, is more adaptable to in-context tasks outside its initial domain. Additionally, we demonstrate that a model tailored through data augmentation can display improved robustness and performance under perturbations. Our work presents a new perspective on the role of training datasets in the development of language models and could influence the creation of future models and datasets in the NLP community. Galaxy cluster observations have recently been marred by the disappearance of numerous cold, gas-poor galaxies. This study endeavors to comprehend the role of radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction in the evolution of gas clouds within a cosmological context, focusing on their interaction with the surrounding hot cluster environment. To this end, we employed cosmological simulations incorporating real galaxy potentials to examine the long-term, three-dimensional evolution of cold clouds under various magnetic field strengths and thermal conduction efficacy. The results indicate that high thermal conduction leads to the early destruction of clouds, while magnetic fields delay cloud formation by reducing their growth rate in the presence of moderate levels of magnetic fields. Conversely, the suppression of thermal conduction by a factor of 10 to 100 leads to cloud survival for an extended period. Moreover, the ambient magnetic field strength significantly affects cloud dynamics, with the partial suppression of thermal conduction allowing for the survival of clouds even in the presence of strong magnetic fields. The simulation's findings align with the observed cold gas content in galaxies within the Coma cluster. The survival of clouds under the simultaneous action of magnetic fields and reduced thermal conduction may be attributed to cloud fragmentation, which prevents its complete destruction by thermal conduction. Furthermore, the expansion of clouds due to the accumulation of supernova energy may contribute to their prolonged existence. The suppression of thermal conduction appears to be the most plausible explanation for the observed cold gas content in the Coma cluster, while magnetic fields may play a significant role in enhancing cloud durability. The simulated results suggest that galaxy potential and cloud density significantly affect cloud evolution, with the potential for a binary relationship between these factors and thermal conduction efficacy. The simulation also yields criteria for the survival of clouds based on the relative rates of radiative cooling and thermal relaxation. Optimizing multi-limbed robot motion poses a challenging non-convex problem. We present a multi-stage optimization framework combining convex programming and data-driven relaxation to tackle this issue. To increase problem solvability, we introduce a novel formulation incorporating non-affine trilinear constraints, whose effects are mitigated by deriving and applying tight data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations. These envelope relaxations are leveraged to develop a more efficient algorithm for motion planning. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a 7-limbed robot demonstrating near-optimal performance. Additionally, this approach provides a useful approximation when solving more complex multi-limbed robots' motion planning problems. By assessing the impact of different assumptions on problem complexity, we identify the most effective strategy for optimizing multi-limbed robot motion. This framework's capabilities extend to motion planning problems involving torsional elasticity, which introduces an intricate non-convex aspect to such problems. This challenge is successfully overcome through the integration of a constant gain estimator to model uncertainty and update robot configurations, facilitating problem solvability. This method's utility is showcased by a successful demonstration of autonomous navigation in a 7-limbed robot. Our proposed approach also compares favorably with state-of-the-art motion planning techniques in multi-limbed robots. To validate assumed model parameters, such as gains and robot tolerances, we develop an online testing protocol incorporating performance metrics, such as error, stability, and task completion success rate. This approach enables robust model assessment, streamlining system design, and improving overall system performance. This framework's general applicability is confirmed through assessments of various models, including a 9-limbed and a 11-limbed robot, indicating its potential for motion planning optimization in a wide range of multi-limbed robots. To facilitate widespread adoption, we provide open-source access to our code and model collections. The movement of the hand causes the coffee to act like a nonlinear pendulum, with its period and shape dependent on the amplitude of the movement. The variation in the coffee's angular displacement with time can be broken down into two components - a uniform, constant rate and a nonlinear variation. The nonlinearity arises due to the interaction between the hand's movement and the gravitational force acting on the coffee, which causes it to slope in a particular way. In computer vision, a comprehensive object recognition typically involves understanding a object's spatial orientation as well as its overall shape. Although existing research has made significant progress in category-level object recognition, very few studies have simultaneously addressed orientation and shape classification. When compromising on category-level recognition for more robust pose estimation or vice versa, performance suffers, highlighting a critical need for a unified framework. We introduce an innovative approach that uses a neural network to simultaneously classify an object's pose and shape within a categorical context. We create challenging scenarios to test resilience, including instances with hidden poses and unfamiliar category members. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of our model's performance on the widely-used NJU-SF10K dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results in category-level pose and shape recognition, and surpassing previously published benchmarks for pose estimation tasks. The source code for our model is available at https://github.com/whai-whai/CategoryKeypointNet.git. Experimental results demonstrate that our model excels at both pose and shape classification, even when presented with limited or ambiguous keypoints, making it an ideal choice for resilient category-level object recognition. The proposed method receives a rating of 8.97/10 for its robustness and 8.75/10 for its overall performance. It has potential applications in areas such as robotics, autonomous driving, and content creation using virtual objects. The method's strength lies in its ability to efficiently process various types of keypoints, including just two for every object, thereby reducing the complexity of the task and making it more resilient to keypoint missing or manipulation. The method's resilience is further enhanced by incorporating the relative rather than absolute positions of keypoints, as well as the use of a keypoint pairing layer that looks ahead to future keypoints during training. The method outperforms previous studies on pose estimation by a considerable margin, and demonstrates resilience in a variety of challenging scenarios, including hidden poses and unfamiliar category members. The method's overall performance and robustness were evaluated using various metrics, and we provide a detailed ablation study to aid future research and improve the method's performance. The method was tested on three datasets, including NJU-SF10K, SF-M-100K, and PASCAL-VOC-SF, using 114 different training, validation, and testing splits to ensure a wide range of training and testing samples. The method uses a keypoint-based representation to understand the shape and pose of objects, and was found to perform significantly better than previous studies that used object-based representations. Calculating the mean of this distribution is impossible, and thus traditional confidence intervals are unusable. However, by leveraging the sample median and half-length as an estimator, we develop a confidence interval for the parameter b of the Cauchy distribution. Additionally, we define and provide the formula for the square of the Cauchy distribution's interval estimator, showcasing its consistency and applying this to the parameter b under both simple random sampling and rank-based sampling methods. Furthermore, we illustrate the interval estimator's performance through simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness, particularly in rank-based sampling, and highlighting the importance of accurately determining sample sizes to achieve desired confidence levels and width specifications. The provided R code facilitates the implementation of these methods and simulation results. As an extension, we apply the proposed methods to the location-scale family, obtaining reliable estimates of both location (m) and scale (s) parameters, and thus the standard deviation (σ) as well. The theoretical basis for these methods stems from well-established principles in nonparametric statistics, including the consistency of median-based estimators, as well as the distribution of ranking statistics. The study presents its main findings, supporting previous works on Cauchy distributions, and providing novel contributions to the literature on this topic. The parameter b's confidence interval exhibits variability, but ultimately converges to a specific value, while the square of the Cauchy distribution's interval estimator shows variability at first but eventually becomes stable, and demonstrates consistency both theoretically and practically. This work introduces a cutting-edge linear parameter varying (LPV) loop-shutting approach for enhancing the performance of motion control systems. By incorporating real-time estimation of nonlinear system parameters, the method dynamically adjusts gain values in a way that's optimized for current operating conditions. This optimization enables the system to automatically switch between sensitivity settings, balancing disturbance rejection and tracking accuracy. Unlike traditional fixed or scheduled gain-shifting strategies, the proposed LPV design allows for precise fine-tuning of loop sensitivity, which is crucial for achieving the best possible performance in motion control applications. To facilitate practical implementation, the authors have also developed a simplified version of the LPV algorithm, reducing computational requirements without compromising performance. The effectiveness of the proposed approach was verified through experimental tests on a high-accuracy motion system, which demonstrated improved dynamic performance and increased stability when the loops are shut in comparison to traditional techniques. Additionally, the results show that the proposed LPV design can achieve up to 10 times faster movement responses while maintaining at least the same level of stability as the existing designs. Furthermore, the LPV-based gain-shifting approach enabled the system to automatically adjust sensitivity based on the scale of the incoming commands, which in turn led to increased robustness and improved motion quality. The proposed algorithm, which is focused on motion control, can also be applied to other LPV systems where loop-shifting is required. The key challenges and opportunities related to the practical implementation of the LPV-based control algorithms were discussed, highlighting their potential to revolutionize the field of motion control. The proposed LPV-based approach, which is primarily centered on motion control, can also be applied to other domains where sensitivity adjustments are necessary. A group characteristic known as $R_\infty$ was introduced by Chillingworth and Wirth, 
and it has been explored further by many mathematicians. This characteristic 
essentially means that in a group, the relation $abc = 1$ implies $c = 1$. 
The main goal of this paper is to verify that nilpotent subgroups of the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group $G_n$ satisfy the $R_\infty$ characteristic. 
To confirm this, we adopted an approach by which a group operator could be represented using the group's cyclic generating pair, 
allowing for the translation of group relations into combinatorial terms involving the integers. 
The satisfaction of the $R_\infty$ characteristic can then be interpreted as a combinatorial property, 
involving the non-coincidence of two integers under a specific linear transformation. 
The validity of the $R_\infty$ characteristic for $G_n$ was confirmed through numerical verification for small values of $n$, 
following which an analytical proof could be obtained using only elementary arithmetic operations. 
As a result, we can conclude that all nilpotent quotients of $G_n$ satisfy the $R_\infty$ characteristic. 
The verification also uncovered an interesting unsolved problem in number theory - for natural numbers $a$ and $b$, 
it remains unknown whether the inequality $ab < b(a+1)$ implies $b(b+1) < a(a+1)$. 
The proof that $ab < b(a+1)$ and $a < (b+1)a$ actually implies $b(b+1) < a(a+1)$ can be considered as an instance of the Clifton-Nong generalization of the famous Three Bodies Theorem. 
The theorems obtained in this paper may also have applications in fields such as combinatorial geometry and the theory of linear codes. 
In addition, we have also identified a variety of nilpotent subgroups satisfying the $R_\infty$ characteristic. 
The subgroups of the form $\langle a,b \rangle$ that satisfy $a^m = b^n = 1$ and involve a wide range of parameters $m, n \geq 1$ also satisfy this characteristic. 
In a similar manner, we have also found that certain generalized semidirect products involving cyclic groups satisfy the $R_\infty$ characteristic.

The width of the Z boson is measured with negligible uncertainty, serving as a standard measure of consistency between theory and experiment. The Standard Model predicts a value for the width with an accuracy of approximately 0.0003 MeV, obtained through on-shell analysis. The completion of the LHC program would result in a measurement precision of 0.0003 MeV, achieved by combining data from the LHC and future colliders, including a 100 TeV pp collider, a 100 TeV ep collider, and a electron-positron collider operating at 10 femtobarns, accompanied by a measurement of the Higgs boson branching ratio. The 100 TeV pp and ep colliders contribute to a predicted new physics sensitivity of around 50 TeV, while the electron-positron collider offers the best prospects for discovering new physics up to 30 TeV or 57 TeV in the absence of a 100 TeV pp or ep collider, respectively. The electron-positron collider provides essential insights into the stability of the SM, specifically by measuring the Z resonance at high luminosity and investigating the SM Higgs boson in a search for its potential instability. The combination of measurements from the Z and Higgs bosons allows for a precision prediction of the SM width, potentially uncovering instability, assuming none exists in the extra dimensions. The availability of a 100 TeV pp or ep collider significantly enhances sensitivity, while a sole electron-positron collider might only result in marginal improvements in measuring extra dimensions. Nevertheless, the electron-positron collider remains the best option for discovering new physics, including extra dimensions, within the reach of its 10 femtobarns. In a scenario where extra dimensions are present, the width of the Z boson serves as a reliable indicator of instability, while also facilitating the determination of mass scales associated with the Lee-Wick or pseudo-Lee-Wick theories. Specifically, for a 5 TeV Lee-Wick or pseudo-Lee-Wick theory, the width of the Z boson is measured at 75 and 94 femtobarns, respectively, with the pure spin-3 s-channel amplitude dominating at high luminosity. In a scenario where extra dimensions are not present, the width of the Z boson primarily indicates the existence of unstable massive particles, with the most sensitive searches focused on a 100 TeV pp or ep collider. Ultimately, a 100 TeV pp or ep collider offers the best prospects for discovering new physics

benchmark datasets reveal that our model outperforms existing methods, and our
source code is available at https://github.com ShakedNet/FeatureMappingRNN.

Neural network-based encoders for point cloud structures significantly benefit
from pre-training to enhance their overall performance.  The majority of current
approaches rely on generic data compression techniques that are independent of the
specific data and may lose crucial information unique to the underlying point
cloud models.  Consequently, these methods necessitate a subsequent decoder to
reconstruct the original structure from the compressed code, thereby increasing
the total number of parameters.  To address these limitations, we introduce a new
point cloud format, dubbed Token-Point-Cloud (TPC), that incorporates a novel
transformation for smoothing point clouds in an unsupervised manner.  The TPC
format comprises three layers: the original point cloud, a density function that
describes the spatial relationships within the cloud, and a unique transformation
that captures the distinct features unique to each cloud.  We then develop an
efficient method for smoothing the density and elimination of redundant
information prior to representation.  Furthermore, we design a format-agnostic
decoder to restore the original structure from the compressed code without
requiring specific knowledge of the underlying structure.  The experimental
results demonstrate that our approach surpasses the performance of current methods
while achieving a significant reduction in the total number of parameters.  We
also introduce three new benchmarks to facilitate future research in this area.  The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Chen-5431/TPC.

Since radar signals are difficult to detect, traditional clear-channel assessment (CCA) methods often fail, leading to collisions and repeated transmission attempts. To overcome this challenge, we develop CCA methods for FMCW radar networks, leveraging its characteristics, such as its undetectable hidden terminal property, to establish unique access protocols. Specifically, we introduce an optimization technique to balance energy efficiency and spectrum efficiency, demonstrating the superiority of CSMA over Slotted ALOHA in both theoretical analysis and simulation. This paper explores the impact of noise from a source on the recovery process in signal measurement, focusing on the constraints imposed by the Cramér-Rao bound. It establishes that noise can prevent exact recovery if its effect is equivalent to ambiguity, although this can be alleviated by increasing the number of measurements. Notably, the paper reveals that the optimal number of measurements scales logarithmically with the problem size, $n$, and the degree of ambiguity, $K$. Importantly, the paper identifies a distinct phase where reliable recovery is possible even when noise power exceeds the squared ambiguity bound. This is determined by the sample size, $m$, and specific conditions on the spectrum of the covariance matrix of the measurements. The findings are validated through experiments involving both synthetic and real data, showcasing their practical implications. Additionally, the paper establishes a framework for obtaining a Bayesian estimator that achieves the Cramér-Rao bound with high probability. This framework relies on a novel thresholding technique based on a modified Wasserstein distance and is demonstrated across various examples. Furthermore, the paper provides a companion device to facilitate empirical evaluations of the proposed methods. This device allows for the determination of a Bayesian estimator that is both computationally efficient and achievable through Bayesian sampling. This, in turn, may lead to improved convergence rates in Bayesian EM algorithms. Lastly, the paper conjectures that its findings could be extended to cover more general forms of noise, potentially at the cost of slightly relaxed accuracy guarantees. This extension could have far-reaching implications for the recovery process and is thus worth investigating further. This new class of materials comprises hydrogen and boron atoms in a $p$-block layered structure. Initially, it was suggested that the $p$-block character might be essential for enhancing superconductivity. Since an in-depth review of the used methods and tools is available elsewhere, this paper concentrates on presenting the validation results, along with recommendations for applying this validation technique to other fail-functional systems. This tool presents a versatile model processing capability for analyzing dependability in fail-functional systems. It allows for quick changes to the system model, supporting the efficient deployment of the proposed validation technique. Additionally, the tool provides a user-friendly interface for performing model checking operations. Users can select models from a predefined library, execute checkers, and access the status of model checking operations, including reports and images, via the tool's interface. This tool can also be employed for other applications beyond fail-functional systems. Its source code is available under an open-source license for anyone to use. The tool's functionality can be modified by adding new models, checkers, and other improvements, then shared with the community. The purpose of this paper is to inspire others to apply formal validation techniques to dependability models, as well as contribute to the tool's development by sharing their own approaches, models, and experiences. Finally, the paper provides a summary of the tool's capabilities and recommendations for future work on fail-functional models and the developed processing capability. Recent advancements in high-tech equipment, particularly the GRAVITY system with its combination of four telescopes and sophisticated data processing, has enabled the capture of high-resolution images within the vicinity of the Galactic Center. By utilizing these improvements, researchers have obtained striking images of the region, including a notable shot featuring a binary star located just a short distance from the GC's accretion disk. Upon examination, they discovered an unusual pattern in the star's appearance, suggesting the presence of GRAVITY system limitations. Further analysis involved modeling the effects of the atmosphere and telescope equipment to pinpoint the source of this anomaly. Their findings indicate that this imprecision can be attributed to two primary factors: the capabilities of the system's data processing, referred to as noise, and the inherent properties of the telescope selection process, known as resolution, which is particularly apparent in the case of the binary star's close proximity. Multiple techniques were employed to verify and confirm the accuracy of these findings. It was determined that the current system configuration, specifically the size and disposition of the 10-m telescopes, along with the intermediate data processing, could accommodate an average level of imprecision of around 40 microarcseconds. Their analysis further suggested that the system's data processing, or'signal-to-noise ratio', could potentially be the primary limiting factor in achieving higher precision, with the capability to improve resolution through the addition of more telescopes, up to a maximum of around 10 microarcseconds. Ultimately, these findings enable researchers to refine their strategies for optimizing future GRAVITY system upgrades and enhance its capability to capture even more precise images of the Galactic Center. Additionally, these breakthroughs have significant implications and potential applications in various fields, including astronomy and physics, for example in the observation of binary stars under intense gravitational forces or in the analysis of the Galactic Center's environment and its relationship with its surrounding accretion disk. By leveraging these improvements, researchers can move forward with more precise models and simulations of these complex celestial entities and phenomena. We introduce an optimization problem, called the generalized k-center problem, where customers located at points in a metric space must be assigned to centers with minimal total cost, subject to anisotropic cost functions and capacity constraints. A key research question in this area is establishing a relationship between the cost of finding doubling centers and the cost of finding centers located near customers, which is defined in terms of the freeway dimension. Our study focuses on two cost functions: the doubling cost and the quasi doubling cost. For doubling metrics, we developed an approximation algorithm capable of finding centers within a factor of 12 of the optimal solution, and we demonstrated that this approximation is best possible by showing an intrinsic lower bound of at least 8 in certain situations. We also established a relationship between the doubling dimension and the freeway dimension, showing that a certain ratio is bounded above by 2, and we identified an infinite class of spaces for which this bound is best possible. Our research also considers the specialized case of minimizing quasi doubling costs. Although we were unable to find an approximation algorithm for this problem, we proposed new lower bounds on the parameter q in terms of the freeway dimension, and we demonstrated that this parameter must be at least 4 when considering certain classes of spaces with fixed and constant cost ratios. This paper explores an iterative algorithm for solving systems of polynomial equations, where coefficients are chosen randomly from a uniform distribution within a specific range. Each iteration involves evaluating and reducing the size of variables through simplification, utilizing Puiseux series. By implementing a simple stopping criterion based on the magnitude of partial derivatives, the algorithm can terminate prematurely if further progress becomes unlikely. Our research demonstrates that this iterative algorithm can solve systems of equations with a certain degree of uncertainty, and we prove that this degree of uncertainty is the minimum required to solve such systems. We also provide an estimate of the minimum number of iterations needed to solve systems of a specific size, and we verify this estimate through experimental testing. Our findings show that this algorithm can solve systems of equations efficiently, and we provide an evaluation of its performance for various problem sizes. We also outline potential future research directions and suggest ways to enhance the algorithm's performance. One area for future research involves adapting the algorithm to solve systems of equations with structured coefficients, and another area involves integrating the algorithm with existing methods to solve systems of equations that have a small number of solutions. Additionally, we suggest implementing the algorithm as an open-source software library to provide an alternative to existing methods for solving systems of equations. This could include using the SINGULAR software package, which is a widely used tool for solving systems of equations, as an example. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained. Specifically, formulas for the free energy, entropy, heat capacity, and van der Waals coefficient have been obtained. This model also enables the calculation of key thermodynamic properties and coefficients. Notably, all derived equations are straightforward, analytically precise, and consistent with quantum field theory. By incorporating 't Hooft loops to represent the influence of fermion-antifermion pairs and using the saddle-point method to analyze the effective action of the gauge-field, we are able to derive a set of differential equations defining the spectrum of vector mesons. Our findings reveal that the spectrum exhibits a mass dependence that is linear, rather than the usual Regge trajectory, and that the spacing between consecutive masses increases as momentum grows. Additionally, we have calculated the width of vector mesons at both rest and in motion, and our results indicate that the width increases in direct proportion to the square of the momentum, rather than the fourth power as might be expected. Our research also shows that the ratio of the width to the mass is constant and unaffected by the mass itself. Finally, we have found that the imaginary component of the self-energy of vector mesons is nonzero at zero momentum, indicating a breakdown of the Wess-Zumino relation, and that this discrepancy increases as momentum grows. Our work contradicts the conclusions of Wambach et al. regarding the viability of the Wess-Zumino relation in a similar context. Instead, we have demonstrated that the relation can be satisfied only if the medium is either entirely chiral or entirely antichiral. Furthermore, we have calculated the extent to chiral and antichiral components contribute to the normal and anomalous kinetic terms in the effective action of gauge-field. Our results indicate that the anomalous term is entirely due to the chiral aspect of the medium, whereas the normal term is entirely due to the antichiral aspect. In numerical relativity, initiating and maintaining symmetry is crucial for simplifying calculations, but the constraints of reflection and axisymmetry significantly restrict possible initial conditions. Our goal is to enable the free selection of initial conditions without adhering to these strict constraints, focusing on axisymmetry in particular. We have developed a novel method, called the Cauchy-Thomas-Fermi-Klein (CTFK) approach, allowing the geometric evolution of an initial profile subject to constraints, regardless of its form. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique by applying it to both static and dynamic axisymmetric initial conditions. We successfully removed all constraints, resulting in the ability to use arbitrary initial profiles. We then showcased the capabilities of our technique by modeling known solutions, such as Kerr black holes and thin disks. Our method provides a general approach that can be adapted to address various symmetry conditions and initial condition constraints. It has the potential to broaden the scope of numerical relativity and facilitate the simulation of complex, real-world astrophysical phenomena. We have released a full implementation of our technique within the CTHK library, allowing for use with the existing numerical relativity code, such as the Thansit code. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChanChenCTHK/CTHK by donation. It can also be accessed through the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ChanChenCTHK/CTHK.
